speechtext:
Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime
Minister): Mr. Speaker, I had a word with the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew), the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) and the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) after I heard over the radio this morning the sad news of the death of Mr. A. L. Smith. We all felt that, though it would be a departure from the usual practice of the house, it would be the wish of all hon. members that we ask you to send Mrs. Smith a message of our deep sympathy in her bereavement.
I think there are two principal reasons for such a departure in this case. One is that Mr. Smith was a member of the House of Commons during this very parliament and up to the end of the last session, when he resigned only because the state of his health was such that he felt he could no longer devote to the discharge of his duties the time and close attention that he felt such duties required. And the second, and I think the very compelling reason, is that during the six years of his membership he had, by his great qualities of intellect, of humour and of warm-hearted love of his fellowmen, endeared himself to each and every one of us, and secured in our regard for him a place of high esteem and enduring affection.
I trust, Mr. Speaker, that you also will feel it is proper to make this departure from our usual practice, and convey to Mrs. Smith the expression of our condolences and of our lasting admiration for a dear personal friend, a distinguished citizen, a great lawyer and a great parliamentarian.

speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: THE LATE ARTHUR L. SMITH TRIBUTE TO FORMER MEMBER FOR CALGARY WEST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I know every hon. member will appreciate the very gracious words with which the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) has paid tribute to a dear friend of every one of us. I feel, too, that the exception he has made on this occasion, for the reasons he has explained, will meet with the approval of all hon. members.
I know that the death of Mr. Smith is a shock to every one of us, because by his gaiety and wit, combined with his wisdom,
he left upon the minds of members of the house an impression which certainly will not be forgotten during the lifetime of any of us.
I had the privilege of being with him in his home just a little over two weeks ago, and I thought he looked better than he had at any time since he was compelled to leave here last spring, owing to ill health. The occasion of two weeks ago was a typical evening in the Smiths' home. His family were there.
I believe all who knew him well-and that would include members of the House of Commons-realized that it was one of the most closely-knit families one would find.
Every afternoon his son and daughter would drop in and, with that familiarity which expresses respect, in recent years they always addressed their father and mother as Sarah and Art, as indeed all the rest of us did.
I know that those who do not belong to the party to which he belonged will not misunderstand me when I say that, when I saw him last, he was confident that Carl Nickle would be coming down here; and Mr. Smith had promised to be here on the occasion of the swearing in of the new member. We were all looking forward to the reunion, because I think it may be said with confidence that no member of the House of Commons has more completely shared the affection of all members than did Art Smith during the years he served here.
Through his service in the House of Commons he made a great sacrifice, a very great sacrifice indeed, for his own community and for Canada. As the Prime Minister has said, he was an outstanding lawyer. His name is associated with some of the most famous cases in western Canada; and it was only a compelling sense of public duty that persuaded him to offer himself for service in the House of Commons.
I believe it may be said that in some measure his life was probably shortened by the fact that he was compelled to be away from those surroundings which meant so very much to him. He and his wife were fond of music, were fond of fellowship, were fond of simply being with other people and sharing ideas about the daily things that happened and that meant so much to every one of us.
He was known in his early days as Sport Smith. I recall that fact because one of the causes of his great popularity was that in

The late Arthur L. Smith everything he did, whether by way of witty comment or of sharp criticism, he was always a sport in the very best meaning of that word.
Calgary has lost an illustrious son and Canada has lost a truly faithful public servant. I know that all of us would wish to join in the expression of sympathy to his wife and family. We would wish particularly to convey to his wife Sarah the thought that all members of this house who knew him so well are in some measure sharing her sorrow at this time. I think we will all hope that there may be some very real comfort in that knowledge.
Because it is so difficult to realize that this gay and vital personality is gone, it seems natural to close these remarks with the sort of expression we might have used in our ordinary meetings: Good-bye, good old Art, we will be thinking of you.

maintopic: THE LATE ARTHUR L. SMITH TRIBUTE TO FORMER MEMBER FOR CALGARY WEST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure that every member of this house joins in the gracious tributes paid by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) to the memory of one who not only adorned this chamber but who often enlivened a dull evening with a witty contribution. Only ten days ago I happened to be in the west and I spoke to Mr. Smith over the telephone. He told me how well he was feeling and I was very glad indeed to know that the rest was doing him good.
We shall long remember him. Regardless of our political differences in this house we do admire a bonny fighter, a man of courage and of wit, as he was. Mr. Speaker, we join with all others in this house in extending to Mrs. Smith, a charming personality herself, and to his family our heartfelt sympathy in their loss.
He was always busy, kindly, interested and friendly. I think it might be fitting to say that we all hope and pray he may rest in peace.

maintopic: THE LATE ARTHUR L. SMITH TRIBUTE TO FORMER MEMBER FOR CALGARY WEST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, those who have preceded me have in fact spoken for all of us. There is little that I 'can add to what has been said already by way of tribute to this great man except to say that while I was a member of the Alberta government I was more or less closely associated with Art, who was the crown prosecutor in Calgary for a good many years. During those years of close association I learned to admire his great capacity, his great abilities and to know him for the lovable character he was.
(Mr. Drew.]

When I came to the House of Commons and shared with him membership in this assembly I learned to love him even more. On behalf of our group I want to say that we do join in the gracious and loving tributes that have been paid this morning to our departed friend, and join with others in extending to Mrs. Smith and the family our deep regrets and assuring them that we are with them in spirit at this time of their trouble.

maintopic: THE LATE ARTHUR L. SMITH TRIBUTE TO FORMER MEMBER FOR CALGARY WEST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe I knew Art Smith better than anyone else in the house. We were elected to the House of Commons at the same time in 1945. We came down to Ottawa together and occupied the same office throughout the time he was a member. Probably no two men ever enjoyed a closer, finer and more harmonious political partnership and friendship, one which to me was an education and inspiration. Art Smith had an extraordinarily quick mind and an unusual gift of expressing his ideas in forceful and clear language. His wit was proverbial in this house and in Calgary, and I think probably I can say throughout the country.
His death is a great shock and a great loss to all of his very wide circle of friends. I wish to join with others in offering my deepest sympathy to his wife and family and to express my own grief at the loss of a great friend and a great Canadian.

maintopic: THE LATE ARTHUR L. SMITH TRIBUTE TO FORMER MEMBER FOR CALGARY WEST
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as Art Smith's deskmate, perhaps I may be allowed one word. He had the unique gift of winning the love and admiration of all who knew him and I am sure that none of us here will ever forget him.

maintopic: THE LATE ARTHUR L. SMITH TRIBUTE TO FORMER MEMBER FOR CALGARY WEST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as one of the senior members of the house I wish to join with those who have paid such fine and well-deserved tributes to our departed friend. You must remember, sir, the evening when you were kind enough to call me over the telephone to invite me to a reception you were giving for the late Mr. Smith after he had delivered his famous farewell speech in the House of Commons. That speech will always be considered as a classic example of parliamentary eloquence. I had the privilege through you of meeting Mr. Smith for the last time with some of his friends in your study. At the time he was suffering from the illness which took him away, but he was just as genial, kindhearted and thoughtful as ever. I had one more occasion, thanks to you, to appreciate his serene philosophy of life.

Mr. Smith was an outstanding member of the bar, of the Canadian Bar Association and of the House of Commons of Canada. He made a success in each field that he entered. Why? Because, as has been so well said, not only was he gifted with a powerful intellect, he had a big and generous heart. This is the reason why this faithful servant of the people before the bar of his province and of Canada at large, as well as in the House of Commons of Canada, belongs to a legion. He will belong forever, like Tommy Church and others of my dear friends, to that legion. Why? Because he has done his duty and because he has been so generous and kind to all. I wish to convey my heartfelt sympathy to his charming wife, Mrs. Smith, to his children, and to his roommate and closest friend in the House of Commons, the hon. member for Calgary East.
Right Hon. J. G. Gardiner (Minister of Agriculture:	Mr. Speaker, I am sure many
of those who were associated with Art Smith in the days when he was "Sport" Smith would expect me as one of two members of this house who were of the group to express a word on their behalf. The hon. member for Fort William was associated with him in the days when he became known as "Sport" Smith in the college life of the city of Winnipeg. I myself had the privilege, and it was a privilege, of engaging in contests with him on the football field in Regina as long ago as 1904 and 1905. From then until the time he left this house a very close understanding and friendship existed between us.
Reference has been made to the fact that he thought quickly. Anyone who ever contested with him in sport on the football field or on the hockey ice knows that his quick thinking was not only a fact of recent years. He was one of the most effective players of his time and earned the title of "Sport" Smith because of his quick thinking followed by action on the football field and hockey ice. I am sure all those who were about his own age and who are still with us would expect me as one who knew him in those days, and who was associated with him, usually on an opposing team, to say a word of appreciation of the long association we had with him as athletes in the early days and in politics in later years. I do not need to say that I have already sent a message of personal sympathy to Mrs. Smith, and am very anxious to join with members of the house in extending the sympathies of the whole house to the family of one who was appreciated, respected and liked, both in his days of sport and in his active political life, by opponents and those who were associated with him as well.

REFERENCE TO EDITORIAL IN "LE DEVOIR"
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege in order to call the attention of the house to an editorial published in yesterday's he Devoir. This newspaper criticizes certain remarks I made in this house on the Canada Elections Act. The writer of this article expresses opinions which differ from mine; that is his privilege. There is however one statement against which I wish to protest most energetically. It is stated there that French is only my second language.
Mr. Speaker, I flatter myself that I speak French and English with equal facility but if there is one language which is most assuredly not a second language with me it is French. I have learned French as a child, in my own home; my whole upbringing has been in that language.
I was a student in the Quebec seminary for eight years and at Laval university for three more. All my studies, in these two institutions, were carried out in French.
That is why I wish to put matters right and to state, most emphatically, that French is certainly not a second language with me.

speechtext: I wish to direct a question to the Minister of National Defence. speakeroldname: Hon. Brooke Claxton (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: USE OF WELFARE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have nothing to add to what has already been said in that connection. There is, we believe, neither occasion nor opportunity for using the welfare agencies in action in Korea. There is only one there, which is a small unit of the Salvation Army, which was in Japan with the Australian occupying forces, and it moved with the Australian regiment to Korea. There are no other welfare agencies. No responsible person who has been there has recommended to me that there should be any welfare agencies. In fact, the only recommendations regarding welfare we have received from responsible people who have been there are to the effect that friends of the troops should write more often, more local news should be sent, and there should be Canadian entertainment.

This is an amendment to section 7 of the act, which has to do with the powers of the president. It is a cutting down of the powers, and the amendment reads as follows:

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES

speechtext: The house resumed, from Monday, December 17, consideration of the motion of Mr. Garson for the second reading of Bill No. 36, to amend the Combines Investigation Act.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house rose last night I had dealt with the fact that the government has denied us the right to obtain evidence of the effect of price maintenance on prices in Canada, so that we are in no position to determine whether or not it hurts the consumer. I had then shown that there is no evidence that its elimination would result in a reduction in the cost of living; whereas there is

Combines Investigation Act evidence that the number of items which are subject to price maintenance, and which enter into the cost of living index, is practically negligible. Therefore we are absolutely without evidence from which to make up our minds whether this practice hurts or helps the consumer, and certainly without evidence on which to base the harsh criticisms made by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) last night.
The government's whole approach to this problem has been to raise great hopes in the minds of the public that they will do something to reduce living costs. Having raised those hopes they find themselves impotent to act effectively, and they are now seeking a way out of their awkward position by an attempt to make a scapegoat of the small retailer who relies on price maintenance for his protection. If this bill passes it will be at the expense of the retail merchant who is being condemned unheard.
I quoted the evidence of Mr. Fred McGregor, the star witness for the government's case, to the effect that it is not the manufacturer who wants or benefits most from this practice, but the retailer. This fact should be most carefully assessed. It shows the error of those government propagandists who seek to whip up prejudice by painting a picture of greedy manufacturers weaving a web of control over the whole economy. The truth is that the system of price maintenance was worked out by the small retailers as a means of self-protection against the power of big interests. In the absence of any conclusive proof to the contrary-and certainly none has been offered
-our position is that anything which preserves and promotes a system whereby trade in Canada is shared amongst a large number of independent businesses, and prevents a further concentration of control in the hands of a few powerful interests, is in the longterm interests of our general economy, including the consuming public.
Before passing on to the next consideration, that is the extent to which the retailer may be harmed if this legislation passes, I think we should mention the fact that, while there is no positive evidence that the principle itself is harmful, there is some evidence which we did manage to get on the record- even though the government resisted-to show that the practice has been beneficial in a small way. I should like to refer to some figures in this respect, but without drawing general and sweeping conclusions from them as the minister was prepared to draw last night from the few figures which he put on the record. I feel it is important to have them before the house so that it can be shown that there are figures which tend to establish that price maintenance is not harmful but rather beneficial to the consumer.
I would refer particularly to the table which appears at page 787 of the committee's proceedings. It was furnished to us by the Retail Hardware Association of Ontario. I would ask the permission of the house, Mr. Speaker, to place this table on Hansard as it appears in the committee proceedings.

I believe it can be said that there is evidence to the effect that price maintenance, instead of hurting the consumer in those respects, benefits him.

There are two other tables to which I should like to refer. The first is found on page 641 of the committee's proceedings, and is a table submitted by the Canadian Association of Radio and Appliance Dealers. They show the profit margin as between price-maintained and non-maintained goods. For washers they show an average discount under resale price maintenance of from 30 to 35 per cent, and for non-price-maintained, of from 40 to 46 per cent; for electric stoves, the price-maintained average was 33J to 37J per cent, and the non-price-maintained average was from 30 to 50 per cent. For refrigerators, the comparable figures are 30 to 35 per cent against an average of from 35 to 50 per cent on non-maintained items.
The next table, beginning at page 643 of the committee's proceedings, is of particular interest since the Minister of Justice last night stated as a fact, without any evidence to support it, that resale price maintenance effectively eliminates competition. I am not going to go into detail on this point, but I do wish to state that that was a conclusion which was not warranted by the evidence before us. The evidence before us shows that, though there is a restriction on competition in one way, that is vertically, in effect there is created a greater and more effective competition between manufacturers and retailers of competing lines. This tendency is borne out by the table appearing on page 643 of the committee's proceedings. It shows that in the field of the electric appliance manufacturing industry, which has been so much condemned because it follows this practice of price maintenance, far from there being too little competition there is as much competition as in any other field, if not more. In the field of radios there are over seventy different brands competing generally in Canada; in electric refrigerators twenty-eight different brands; electric stoves, twenty-three different brands competing in Canada; and in electric washing machines, seventy-five different brands all competing for the market. It simply cannot be said, therefore, that resale price maintenance eliminates competition when you have that number of brands competing in the Canadian market, unless the minister is prepared to say that, for instance, some seventy-three makers of washing machines have all united to form a gigantic combine to eliminate competition between them. If that is the inference we are to draw from the minister's remarks, it is a sorry reflection upon his administration of his own department, and the efficacy of the combines administration branch, which latter implication I for one do not accept.


We have seen that there is an almost complete lack of evidence as to whether harmful effects follow from this practice of price maintenance. On that basis we submit there is no justification for taking the drastic steps contemplated by this legislation. This position is reinforced by the fact that there is specific and convincing evidence of the dangers and disadvantages which will follow to the small retailer. I have mentioned the fact that it is not the big manufacturer but the small retailer who designed and wishes to maintain the assistance of this practice, as shown by the evidence of Mr. McGregor, where he said the person who wants it and benefits most is, unquestionably, the retailer, not the manufacturer.
I should like to refer to the evidence contained in the brief submitted by the president of the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada, as reproduced at page 380 of the proceedings of the committee. In the brief which he submitted, Mr. Bengough pointed out that in the view of the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada the elimination of resale price maintenance, far from increasing competition, might in fact lessen it to the detriment of the independent operator. Here is what Mr. Bengough said:
Before accepting these general conclusions without reservation, it might be worthwhile to consider what would happen in specific cases when and if the law is amended to make resale price fixing practices illegal. Take for example two large manufacturers of men's clothing. The one manufacturer owns or controls, or owns and controls, his retail outlets. He, of course, has full control of the resale prices of his products. The other manufacturer operating in direct competition with the first does not own any retail outlets. He, however, provides services to those independent retailers who handle his products and, as well, fixes the resale price of his goods. If the practice of resale price maintenance is ruled illegal, it would seem fairly obvious that the second manufacturer would be required to cease his present practices. Would the first be required to stop fixing the retail price of his goods which are sold through his own retail stores? If the answer to this question is in the negative, then will not the result of the new law be to reduce effective competition in the men's clothing trade rather than to strengthen it?
Perhaps the most conclusive evidence that it is the little man that wants this resale price maintenance as a form of self-protection is to be found in the fact, already referred to, that the big men represented by Eaton's and one or two other large department stores have come out definitely as being opposed to the practice.
Upon the question of whether or not there is in fact danger of disaster to the small retailer if price maintenance should be eliminated, it must be recognized at the outset that there is a great deal of conflicting opinion. There is much theory, based upon a difference in economic circumstances

between now and former years, and alleged differences in trading conditions which that brings about, enlarged upon by the minister and particularly emphasized by Mr. Fred McGregor who, as I have pointed out, based his whole opposition to resale price maintenance exclusively on theory and who rejected any consideration of fact and physical results in arriving at his conclusion. There is much theory to the effect that the elimination of this practice will not adversely affect the retail merchant-that is, the elimination of price maintenance-because, it is said, loss leaders cannot arise under present day conditions.
Mr. Speaker, I do not question the right of members of this house to form opinions and conclusions. Indeed, it is our responsibility to do so. I say, however, that we should place ourselves in possession of the facts before being asked to form those conclusions; and we are not in possession of the facts. But while I certainly believe that it is our right and our duty to form conclusions, I also believe that the person who is in the best position to form a correct and accurate conclusion as to what will be the effect upon him of legislation eliminating price maintenance is the retail merchant himself who has experienced the lack of resale price maintenance in the past and who is going to experience it in the future if this legislation is passed. I make no bones about it that I would rather accept the opinions and the conclusions of these gentlemen, based upon their practical experience, than the conclusions and theories, based upon considerations of policy only, of those who have absolutely rejected any question of fact in arriving at their conclusion.
We have had evidence from many independent retailers to the effect that they will be disastrously affected by the practice of loss leadering at the hands of the big stores, if price maintenance is eliminated. In the proceedings of the committee there are certain passages that I think I should read in this connection, but before doing so, as perhaps the most authoritative statement of the dangers and the evils of the practice of loss leadering, I should like to quote a statement from the report of the royal commission on price spreads of 1935, at pages 228 and 229. In the chapter dealing with distribution we find these passages; and I am going to take the liberty of placing them on the record at some length because, as I say, they are the most authoritative statements of the effects and the evils of this practice in Canada. They start by saying:
One of the most common practices of modern merchandising is the use of "leaders" or "loss leaders".
Combines Investigation Act
Then they go on to say:
Special mention must be made of the disastrous effect of loss leaders on the primary producer. The use, for example, of butter as a loss leader was proved to be a very widespread practice. Since a reduction in the price of butter will not perceptibly increase its consumption, this practice very definitely causes a loss to the dairy producer that far outweighs any possible gains to the consumer. This is equally true of other standard agricultural products. Their use as loss leaders establishes, as customary, a price that reacts to the detriment of the primary producer.
May I pause here to interject that it is a fact that marketing legislation, such as we know it, to an increasing degree has been designed to protect the agricultural producer, and those dependent upon the agricultural economy, against this vicious practice of loss leadering, amongst other things, and to protect him in general from unfair competitive practices. Then they go on to say:
Likewise, a manufacturer, who has built up a wide demand for his products, is injured when these are regularly sold1 at cut prices. Because the profit margin is thereby lost on such goods, competitors of the price-cutter lose interest in the goods and push more profitable lines.
Then they go on to point out the dangers to the consumer that result from this practice, and they emphasize the point that although the consumer may get some small immediate benefit-although that itself is questionable, owing to factors which they emphasize-in the long run the consumer suffers. They emphasize that point as follows, and I am now reading at page 229:
The consumer who purchases goods at cut prices undoubtedly gains on those items. But leaders-
That is, loss leaders.
-are offered primarily to draw the public and create the impression of similar value as applied to goods on which prices have not been cut. While the difficulties of judging quality and price are growing with the increasing use of branded and trademarked articles, the average purchaser can pick out the "loss leaders" from the other goods offered; otherwise there would not be the same widespread use of this device.
Then they go on:
The competitors of the store using the "loss leader" are, however, the persons chiefly affected.
Those are -the persons that I am dealing with at the moment: the competitors of the big stores who use loss leaders. I continue:
That the deliberate use of cut prices to draw patronage away from competitors is an unfair trade practice, is quite clear. Such reductions are not prompted by any desire to serve the public by giving lower prices. One purpose is to attract customers to whom the store hopes to sell goods that are not loss leaders, at substantial profits. Another purpose is to create the illusion of lower prices on all articles. That this end is not always attained does not in any way lessen the unfairness of the practice.
They then go on to say:
As independent merchants, singly, cannot meet the leaders of chain stores, many have joined the voluntary associations already described. By acting

together, such groups of merchants can and do follow practically the same policy of using "loss leaders" as is pursued by the corporate chains. Those independent merchants who are not members of such associations are, therefore, subjected not only to the unfair competition of chain stores but also to that of voluntary chains.
Surely nothing could make more clear the danger that, by eliminating resale price maintenance-the only protection the retailer now has against the practice of loss leader-tog-the effect will be not to increase competition but, on the contrary, more and more to drive merchants into organizations, associations or chains, either voluntary or compulsory, whose only effect and whose only purpose would be in fact to decrease competition. That emerges most clearly from this considered statement of principle of the royal commission on price spreads. They conclude as follows:
We condemn the practice of loss leaders as unfair, promoting wasteful competition and seriously affecting the income of certain classes of primary producers.
Then they go on to mention the difficulties of designing effective legislation against loss leaders.	I shall have something to say
later about the question of the difficulty of legislating against it.
Then, so far as the evidence before our committee is concerned, let me refer particularly to the evidence given by Mr. Bengough at page 372, where it says:
Q. What is your view, would you agree that it would only be fair, if we are going to introduce legislation to outlaw in blanket fashion all price maintenance agreements, that we should at the same time introduce legislation to prevent the loss-leader practice?

I think it would be vital it should be done.
And then there was further evidence from the retail merchants. I refer to the evidence of Mr. Preston, who was secretary-manager of the Canadian Pharmaceutical Association. At page 132 of the proceedings of the committee we And this passage-and it should be noted that for many years Mr. Preston was a practical retailer before assuming the position he now holds. He referred to the length of time that the loss-leader device has been in effect, in this fashion:
The loss-leader device is not a new device; it has been in practice particularly in the province of Ontario since the turn of the century, and the only effective means that has been found so far to curb it is price maintenance as we know it today.
We maintain that without price maintenance the loss leader would be on our doorstep tomorrow and chaotic conditions similar to those in the 1920's would result.
Mark that-not the 30's, but the 20's, when there was chaotic condition in the retail trade. He goes on to say:
We do not like monopolies; they are bad for the country, whereas the independent merchant is the

backbone of every village, town and hamlet. Surely the government will do nothing to hurt him.
Unfortunately Mr. Preston's confidence in the present government is not justified.
Then he proceeds to give some specific examples of how it operates. At page 147 we find this statement by Mr. Preston:
A. No. That is right. The loss leader in the drug business has been a thing sold at crazy prices. For example, I have sold Baby's Own Soap which sold normally for 10 cents, and when we opened our stores we sold it at 1 cent-we started off at 5 cents and the independent druggist thought he could beat us and he cut the price to 4 cents; then we brought it down to 3 cents and he sold it at 2 cents, and, finally, we sold it at 1 cent, and we did that-I say "we", I mean the chain store-"we" put that independent druggist right out of business, and he was a good solid citizen, a member of the city council in the city of Toronto. That is loss-leader.
And continuing with the evidence of Mr. Preston at pages 151 and 152:
A. Well, we assume that the minute the government were to legislate against price maintenance every article that is now price-maintained would become overnight a loss leader.
And again:
A. Yes, sir, and that is why it was very difficult to operate a retail drug store in the urban centres prior to price maintenance. It was almost impossible to make a fair living.
Sir, I submit that those answers from a practical man, a man as well qualified to draw conclusions as most other people would be, if not more so, demonstrate clearly, quite contrary to the theories which have been advanced to the effect that loss leadering could not occur at the present time, that there is imminent danger of loss leadering if this legislation passes. There is no other protection available to the retail merchants against the practice of loss leadering. That has been most clearly established by the evidence.
Here I would observe that our committee, in its majority report, which was dissented from by all the members of the official opposition, says that there is an effective answer to the practice of loss leadering, in section 498A of the Criminal Code. That statement was supported in his speech last night by the Minister of Justice.
Let me point out that the opinion of these theorists-for the minister advanced nothing but theory-is contradicted by the opinion- not just the opinion, but by the factual statement-of the government's star witness, Mr. Fred McGregor.

I have just pointed out that the government majority on the committee, along with the Minister of Justice, have stated that there is adequate protection against the practice of loss leadering, in section 498A of the Criminal Code. However, the star witness for their case, the man who has had more experience than any other man in Canada in dealing with combines, the man who was combines commissioner for twenty-five years, before his resignation was forced upon him by the government, has stated clearly that section 498A is no answer at all to the danger of loss leadering.
Let me read from his evidence as it is set out at page 604. At that point there had been some discussion as to whether or not there was danger of loss leadering if price maintenance was eliminated. We had been asking him whether or not in fact there could be legislation which would be effective against

Mr. McGregor referred to the efforts to deal with loss leaders by legislation, in the form of certain provincial statutes. Then, in connection with the British Columbia statute, I took the opportunity of saying:
It just does not work. It had to be made so full of holes it just does not work.
This is the answer by Mr. McGregor:
A. That is the difficulty of producing any bill that will work, and that is the point I am stressing here. It is exceedingly difficult to draft legislation that will prevent these practices we have in mind and still not injure the public in a serious way.
The "practice we had in mind" was the practice of loss leadering.
The next question and answer were as follows:
Q. You said on Wednesday, in answer to a question from me, that it could be done. You are not now going back on that, are you?
A. I said that lawyers should be able to produce something. I still think they may. We were not able to do it in our struggles with the problem.
Mr. McGregor was the combines commissioner when section 498A was placed on the statute books. He did not refer us to a single prosecution under section 498A and at no point did he say, when under questioning about loss leadering, that that section was the answer to that practice. But he did say that they had not been able to design effective legislation against the practice of loss leadering.
Then we have the report of the price spreads commission, which deals with this matter at page 229, and I quote as follows:
We condemn the practice of loss leaders as unfair, promoting wasteful competition and seriously affecting the income of certain classes of primary producers, but in seeking a solution for the problem through legislative remedies we are confronted with certain difficulties.
They then point out that you have to make so many exceptions to meet legitimate cases of reduced prices that your legislation becomes practically unworkable.
I rely not only on those authorities but on other authorities as well. Perhaps these authorities will be acceptable to the Minister of Justice and the hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Sinclair), because they are authorities of the Liberal party. When section 498A was discussed in the house in 1935 we had clear and specific statements from prominent Liberal authorities, both lawyers, that the section as then enacted was completely unworkable, was absolutely useless, and that we should not even bother to put it on the statute books. I refer first to the statement by Colonel Ralston. I do not think

If I may have the floor for a minute I will answer. Everything that was said in our committee by the government members and by the government experts who were before us indicates to me that although Colonel Ralston's language was a little strong nevertheless it is true that the effects of section 498A were not those which the government introducing it had hoped would follow. I would point out further to my hon. friend that the government introducing it itself expressed doubts as to whether section 498A would be effective, but they had the courage to attempt to find an answer. They were not afraid to try something. They introduced this legislation.
But now, when they are on the spot my hon. friends, whose party in 1935 expressed these derogatory opinions about the effectiveness of the legislation, are the ones who are wiggling; they are the ones who are now taking the opposite view and talking big and saying that section 498A is the complete answer to the practice of loss leadering.
I come now to another Liberal authority, a former minister of justice. I would ask the present Minister of Justice if he disagrees with the opinion expressed by one of his predecessors, a member of his own party. Here is what Mr. Ilsley had to say about the


efficacy of this section, and I quote from page 3487 of Hansard as follows:
To put the matter very briefly I should say it would be a mistake to pass subsection A of section 498, which is found in section 6 of the bill.
And then at page 3488:
Very little care has been exercised in the drafting of this section; apparently whoever drafted it had only a superficial view of the problem before him.
And again at page 3489:
I do not know that I have very much more to say with regard to this section, but I consider it so far short of anything that is useful that I do not think this subsection should be passed.
I confront the Minister of Justice with the same question that he has just asked me- and which I have answered. I have said that I do not think section 498A is as efficacious as those who introduced it had hoped it would be. It has not worked and I do not think it will work. I point out that those who were introducing it at the time had the courage to say that they were not certain about this, that they had given it the best consideration they could, but they were not stating as a fact that it would work.
I ask the Minister of Justice whether he is dissenting from and condemning the opinions expressed by Colonel Ralston, an eminent lawyer, and by the Hon. Mr. Justice Ilsley, who was his predecessor but one in the office which he now holds? If not-and there is no answer-then we must rely upon the opinions of those two Liberal statesmen, one a former minister of justice of this government, and it becomes perfectly apparent that to eliminate the practice of price maintenance, as will be done by this legislation, will leave the retail merchant absolutely exposed and without any protection against the practice of loss leaders. I submit to you and to the house that nothing could more amply demonstrate the folly and unfairness of enacting this legislation without giving this problem adequate consideration.
And so I come back to what I referred to last night. The majority report of the committee says that if the elimination of price maintenance does affect the trade of the retail merchants the government will keep careful watch on it and then work out some other legislation. Against that I point out that Mr. McGregor says that we have never been able to design effective legislation in all our struggles with the problem.
It certainly seems an irresponsible, rash and unfair attitude on the part of the government that is administering the affairs of this country to say, "We are not certain what the results of this will be; but if the result of eliminating price maintenance is to expose

the retailer to the effects of loss leaders, then we will enact some legislation to try to fix up the matter." I ask the Minister of Justice whether the government will undertake to restore the bankroll of the merchant who has gone bankrupt? Will he include that in his legislation? Will he restore the position of the merchant who has suffered in the meantime while the Minister of Justice is making this diagnosis to find out whether his own cure has killed the patient? If the government will say that they will take the responsibility of seeing that no merchant goes bankrupt as a result of having eliminated this protection, then perhaps one could support the position. But until the minister says that, until the minister is prepared to guarantee his medicine, in fact, to take his own medicine, I say the legislation should not be supported.

And so we are left with the conclusion that there is no evidence to show that the legislation will benefit the consumer; but there is evidence that it will harm the retailer. I should like to refer now to the type of harm which will follow from the enactment of this bill. Because it is significant that certain of the large departmental stores are ' supporting this legislation, I think we should refer to some of the findings of the royal commission on price spreads with respect to the predominant position which these stores enjoy in the economy of Canada. On page 207 of the report of the royal commission, in the chapter on "Distribution" and under the heading, "Possibilities of Future Expansion", we find the following:
The concentration of business in the hands of a few companies is far greater in Canada than in any other country for which information is available. In the United States in 1929 there were seventeen companies operating 2,400 department stores with sales of $1,500 million. The sales of these seventeen organizations, however, represented only 34 per cent of the total department store business in the United States whereas the three largest companies in Canada handle 80 per cent. The largest single department store and mail-order organization in the United States, Sears Roebuck and Company, had less than one per cent of the total resale business in that country, while in Canada the T. Eaton Company had more than 7 per cent.
More than 7 per cent of all retail business in Canada is done by one company alone, the T. Eaton Company. They go on to say:
It is interesting to note that the largest retail organization in Canada is in the department store and mail order field, while in the United States the largest organization is in the grocery and meat chain field. But even this company, the Great Atlantic and Pacific Tea Company, with sales of approximately $1 billion in 1929, did not occupy as dominant a position in the United States as did the T. Eaton Company Limited in Canada.
Combines Investigation Act
The fact is, Mr. Speaker, that the elimination of resale price maintenance opens up again all the possibilities of loss leadering and unfair trade practices against which merchants have devised their own protection under the system of price maintenance, and exposes them to the increasing concentration of power in the hands of a few concerns. On this point the commission had this to say, as found at page 232, as to the concentration of power in a few hands:
The concentration in retail distribution already achieved has had certain undesirable effects. Socially, it has meant that in approximately one-third of the retail business of this country, the personal factor has largely disappeared with the inevitable weakening of the ideals of service to the community, so long and honourably associated with the local independent store. That such a development has occurred in other phases of economic life makes it nonetheless to be regretted in the field of distribution.
Then they express this opinion which I think should be pondered well by the government and this house before we pass this legislation. They say:
We would add, however, that monopoly or quasimonopoly in the vitally important field of retail distribution, could not be regarded by any government with equanimity. A sound regard for the national interest could not permit two or three concerns to dictate the method of retail distribution in the country as a whole.
On that point I pause here to mention that the T. Eaton Company has very considerably expanded its business in Canada by the purchase recently of all the David Spencer Limited stores throughout British Columbia. Therefore we can see that Eaton's, which did 7 per cent of all retail business in Canada in 1929, is probably doing a considerably increased percentage today. Thus we have this position: it emerges that the result of this legislation may not be, in fact probably will not be, to preserve or promote competition in the retail field, but may in fact be, and probably will be, to increase the tendency towards monopoly of that field. In that respect I should like to quote the opinion of the National Council of Women who share the same views on this subject as we do ourselves. At page 5 of their brief the national council says that they do not agree with the MacQuarrie committee when that committee says that they do not think it imperative to make an immediate and hasty recommendation regarding loss leadering. Their brief goes on to say:
Council believes that competition in free enterprise is a healthy state but it ought not to further less leadering. In other words, what legislation is enacted ought to specifically penalize loss leadering.
May I point out today that our committee did give some thought to this matter. In about an hour and a half's session one

Combines Investigation Act morning we debated the problem of loss leadering. We had before us a recommendation designed by one of the members of the committee; but practically every member of the committee felt that, while his effort to deal with the problem of loss leadering was commendable, he nevertheless did not offer a practical solution of the problem, and indeed many members of the committee, including government members, expressed grave doubts as to whether loss leadering could be dealt with at all by legislation.
I should like to read the further opinion of the Trades and Labour Congress having to do with this subject. It is to be found at page 380 of the committee's proceedings. They had this to say:
One possibility your committee should keep in mind, and, in the opinion of this congress, make every effort to guard against, in any amendments that may be suggested, is a swing of distributive business away from the smaller outlets and a concentration of such trade in a few very large establishments.
Further down on the same page they say:
This raises two very important questions for consideration by your committee: (1) Does this indicate that resale price maintenance does not always lead to reduced competition? and (2) would the banning of resale price-fixing make it impossible for the large distributor to offer his own brands at his own fixed prices? If not. and it is difficult to see how such a law could be made to fit this type of situation, then it would appear that the large distributor would gain a tremendous advantage over the manufacturer without any apparent advantage having been gained by the ultimate consumer. Such a development would merely place more economic power in the hands of the larger distributors. It is hard to see where it would increase effective competition or efficiency. It is even more difficult to see where the public interest would be served.
In addition, as an authority on this point I want to refer to the evidence of Mr. George Hougham, who has the advantage, in addition to that of being an expert, that he comes from the province of British Columbia. Mr. Hougham's evidence is found at pages 766 and 767. Mr. Hougham is a man who has had very extensive experience in the retail trade, a man who was intimately associated with the whole of the Stevens and royal commission inquiries into price spreads, and who is recognized as an expert in his field. I want to read the following questions and answers from page 766, when Mr. Hougham was giving evidence:
Q. In other words, three department stores did 80 per cent of all department store business, but one of them did 7 per cent of all the retail business in the country. Is that right?
A. Yes, I think that is correct, but the report will correct me if I am wrong.
Q. Was that company named?
A. Yes, it was the T. Eaton Company.
Q. Do you know whether that company has since acquired other large retail outlets?
A. Oh, yes, it has.
[Mr. Fulton.1
Q. Where?
A. Notably in Vancouver, where they have taken over David Spencer.
Q. They have taken over the David Spencer Limited business all throughout British Columbia, have they not?
A. Yes.
Q. You are aware, of course, of the fact that the T. Eaton Company has indicated to this committee that they are opposed to the practice of resale price maintenance?
A. Yes.
Q. And I think you have raid already that in your view the elimination of that practice would tend to benefit mainly the large department store?
A. I think that would be the inevitable tendency.
Q. Do you see any connection between those two sets of facts, the T. Eaton Company's attitude and your opinion which you have just expressed?
A. I do not care to impute motives or to make general inferences-I do not think this is amusing, Mr. Chairman-
These words were an aside by Mr. Hougham, who was suffering from the strong attitude of the chairman of the committee, from which we all suffered from time to time. Then I go on with the quotation:

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext:
No, it is certainly not. It is so unusual we are gratified to have you make such a straight statement.
The Witness: But I would think that perhaps-I know I should not be talking for the T. Eaton Company-but that is perhaps the reason they adopt that attitude, the traditional attitude that they do not want to have anybody tell them what to do.
What Mr. Hougham is expressing in those well chosen and reasonable words is that one of the reasons at the back of the mind of the T. Eaton Company in their opposition to price maintenance is probably the fact that it will improve their competitive condition vis-a-vis the small retail dealer. I am not saying that the T. Eaton Company, or any other company, in taking that attitude is doing anything illegal. It is perfectly legal, but I am stating it as a fact, which we have to reckon with, when we are considering the effects of this legislation and when we are considering what will be the position of the small independent retailer as a result of the legislation.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I would like to summarize as follows: We have no evidence that the practice of resale price maintenance is harmful at the present time with respect to its effect on prices; we have no evidence that its elimination will reduce the cost of living. My attitude in this regard is exactly the same as that of the Trades and Labour Congress, as expressed at page 379 of the committee proceedings. They say:
Whatever the committee had in the way of information-
Here he is referring to the MacQuarrie committee. I say this expression of opinion applies to the MacQuarrie committee, the

parliamentary committee, and it also is perfectly descriptive of the situation in which we find ourselves here in this house today. The Trades and Labour Congress in their brief say:
Whatever the committee had in the way of information before it about the extent of the practice of resale price fixing, it certainly didn't present your committee or any other interested party with any concrete evidence on which to base a case either for or against resale price maintenance.
So we have no evidence in that regard. But we have much evidence that it will hurt the small independent retailer. This evidence is based upon the facts that we were presented with as .the past practices in this field. We have evidence that it will bring about increasing concentration of power in a few hands, based upon the report of the royal commission on price spreads. We have evidence that the retailer has no other protection against the practice of loss leadering, except that to be found in the resale price maintenance system; and for those reasons the official opposition recommended that the proper report to be brought into the house by the parliamentary committee was a report along the following lines-and I am here reading the last three paragraphs of the report which was laid before the committee for its adoption, but which was rejected by the government majority on that committee. We suggested the committee report as follows, as shown on page 827 of the committee's proceedings:
Your committee, having been much impressed by the very real concern felt by retail merchants over the danger to them from unfair competition and loss leadering practices by powerful chain and departmental stores if price maintenance is eliminated, is of the opinion that if any legislation is ever to be enacted against the one type of practice it must be accompanied by complementary legislation against the other.
Your committee has been unable, in the time at its disposal, to study and work out legislation which it can confidently recommend as being constitutional and effective to meet the danger of loss leadering.
Your committee therefore reports that it is not in possession of sufficient evidence on which to base legislation and recommends that further careful consideration be given to this whole subject, and particularly to the question of fair trade laws along the lines of those in force in the United States of America, as a proper and workable solution of the problem.
That recommendation which we placed before the parliamentary committee still represents the position of this party.
In the light of the considerations that I have laid before the house in analysing the proceedings of our committee and the factors which emerge from a study of this situation, we can see the folly and unfairness of enacting this legislation at this time and leaving the
Combines Investigation Act small man at the mercy of big business, with no certainty whatsoever of benefit to the consumer.
Just 16 years ago the country was shocked and alarmed at the revelations of the inroads that big powerful chain monopolies had been making into the distributive trade of Canada, at the expense of the small man, and to the detriment of the public generally. As Mr. Hougham said, "When the giants are contending, the little fellow gets trampled underfoot." Price maintenance became generally applied because, as we have seen, it is the only method yet devised by which the little fellow can get protection against the giants. It is all very well for Mr. Fred McGregor, or anyone else, to sneer at the little corner merchant and say he is uneconomic, and callously condemn his distinction-along with the veteran and all others who are just. getting established, because they are weak- just for the sake of some economic theory. But responsible legislatures cannot, or should not, behave in that way.
Yet that is exactly what we are being asked to do in this bill-without sufficient evidence, without adequate consideration, without having given them a fair hearing.
It may be that there are valid objections to price maintenance being left exclusively in the hands of private individuals. But I emphasize the point that it is a protective device, to protect the small legitimate trader and operator against the unfair competition of the strong. As such, it is nonsense to condemn it out of hand as running counter to the private enterprise system. For many years now our efforts-the efforts of the combines act itself-have been to devise laws which will protect the individual and the public generally against the unfair practices of strong combines and monopolies. Restrictions on unfair competitive practices have been one feature of this process. Agricultural organizations, labour unions and others have all pressed for-and received-laws which enable them to organize to protect the weaker individual member against unfair competition from the strong, whether that competition comes from within or without. The retail merchant has done the same thing, not by laws, but by working out the price maintenance system.
And so we say it may be that some form of public protection should be substituted for the private system of price maintenance. The fair trade laws of the United States are an example which we think this house should study and consider, and so do the retailers. But do not take a theoretical position about price maintenance, unsupported by any factual evidence, and throw the retailers to

Combines Investigation Act the wolves of unfair competition by eliminating this protection without substituting any other. In the words of Mr. Hougham, at page 768 of the proceedings:
Then I enter at this stage a most earnest plea to you as a committee and to this government, not to throw the baby out the window with the bath. If you are determined to get rid of this principle then at least give these people some protection against the thing which they fear most, and don't do one without the other.
It is because this bill would do one without the other that we urge the government now, as we did in the committee, to give the house and parliament time to look into the facts of this situation and to devise some effective means of protecting the small retailer. I therefore move seconded by the member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming):
That this bill be not now read a second time, but that it be read a second time this day six months hence.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext:
I do
not propose to join what but for the rules of the house would become a marathon, Mr. Speaker. I am not saying that in any disrespectful way of either the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) or the hon. member who has just taken his seat. Fortunately the rules of the house prevent all other members of this house from engaging in what might otherwise become a marathon. This problem is a difficult problem. It is a problem which has been investigated recently by a committee of this parliament, and it has been investigated over and over again in the United States. It has been the subject of a recent white paper in Great Britain, and is a problem which faces all the legislatures of our various democratic countries. We are no exception in having to face it now.
Resale price maintenance is, of course, a method by which prices are maintained irrespective of the conditions under which the articles are sold. A short time ago I was reading a work on distribution and resale by Professor Henry Smith, the vice-principal of Ruskin college, Oxford. His views have been summarized in a pamphlet published by the Fabian society in Great Britain. I think at the outset of my remarks I shall put a cogent paragraph from that pamphlet on the record. It reads:
If all the shops in the trade, irrespective of their cost of doing business, charge the same protected price, then the price cutter may build up a fictitious reputation for cheapness on the strength of cutting the price of protected goods while he overcharges on others. But it is the system of price maintenance which creates the problem: abolish it and the piratical price cutter (if he is a pirate) will be disarmed.
The evils of the system are twofold. When prices and margins are fixed by manufacturers in association with retailers the two may well be sharing


an abnormally high level of profit. Even when this does not take place, the price which the village or suburban shopkeeper must obtain to cover his expenses is higher than the urban trader needs. Thus either the more favourably placed retailer makes more profit than is necessary, or too many shops come into operation in the centres of population, thus lowering the turnover, putting up the costs, and reducing the profit of others. Profits are reduced, but the consumer is not assisted and manpower is wasted.
I think in a few words Professor Smith places the problem in its proper perspective.
The legislation now before the house is the result of a report of a special committee established by this House of Commons in co-operation with the other place. The immediate cause of the establishment of that committee, as has been said both by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) and by the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) was of course the notification to this house by the government in the speech from the throne that an interim report of the MacQuarrie committee had been received. After studying the combines legislation that committee recommended that suppliers should be prohibited from requiring or inducing distributors to resell goods at fixed or minimum resale prices. In its report the MacQuarrie committee remarked that resale price maintenance had been noted on many occasions during investigations by the combines investigation commission, but usually those notations were made in conjunction with and incidental to investigations of other practices.
There was one investigation in 1927 in which this practice was the sole topic under discussion, and I believe that was an inquiry into the proprietary articles and trade association regulations. Hon. members will recollect that as a result of that inquiry the association was disbanded when the commissioner reported that the public interest was detrimentally affected by that association. May I say that this was also the conclusion reached in other investigations which dealt with certain aspects of the problem; tobacco in 1938; dental supplies in 1947; optical goods in 1948, and bread in western Canada. Consequently, the legislation comes before us as a result of a number of investigations and reports made under the Combines Investigation Act. In other words, it is not before us as a means of preventing increases in the already high cost of living. I do not think it will have a great effect on that. It may have a slight effect, but in any event it is rather an attempt by government and by parliament to deal with something which, from time to time, has been stated to be detrimental to the public interest. It is for that reason the legislation is before us.

Evidence concerning this practice was noted by the royal commission on prices in 1949. Hon. members will recall that commission was a continuance of an investigation started under a special committee of this parliament. This is what that commission stated at page 28 of volume 1 of its report:
Resale price maintenance, like other forms of restrictive practices, does offer what appears to the manufacturer and distributor to be a happy relief from the unending struggle against the harsh correctives of the free market system.
In other words, if we are living under a free enterprise system there are supposed to be certain correctives inherent in that system- I do not always agree that they are there but they are said to be there, and this is an attempt to get around the correctives that are said to be inherent in the system of free enterprise, which my hon. friends all over the house allege from time to time that they support.

-to the extent that when price controls by parliament and under the authority of this parliament or of the legislatures of the country were in effect, the same manufacturers and many but not all of the distributors protested and protested; and so successfully did they do so that finally the government-shall I put it this way, though perhaps some may think I should not do so- bowed to the insistent demands from my hon. friends of the Progressive Conservative party as well as of the manufacturers and some distributors that all control should be abolished. In other words, the enforcement of price control by public bodies was distasteful to those who today are making a protest against this bill which is designed to make illegal the practice of resale price maintenance or a form of price control by private manufacturers and distributors. I think we should keep this fact clearly in mind when we are discussing this problem.
But indeed it goes further than that. In the evidence before this committee and in the evidence before the commissioner under the Combines Investigation Act on many occasions, it has been shown that manufacturers have taken effective steps to enforce what is in effect a "code of law", a code of private law. It has established a private system of law which allows no appeal to any court of justice. I submit-and I think all hon. members will agree with me-that if we are to have in this country any code of law of any
Combines Investigation Act
description, whether that code of law governs prices or otherwise, it should be enacted by legislation of this parliament or of the legislatures of the country, and should be enforced by some public authority.

speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman permit a question on the matter of private law?

speechtext: Yes.

speechtext: Is it not true that what it really is is something in the nature of a contract and that in fact it has been questioned and litigated in the courts frequently?

speechtext: In my opinion, it is a code.

speechtext: A code?

speechtext:
A code; it is a code of law. It is true that persons agree to abide by that code of law laid down by the manufacturers; but because they agree to observe that code does not make it any less a code of law, in effect; and there is no appeal to the courts.
Let me point out that quite recently, in relation to other private interests in this country, a regulatory body, the C.B.C., set up by and operated under a statute enacted by this parliament, was limited by the legislation that was passed as to what it might do since in that legislation we provided that the person regulated might appeal to the exchequer court for a decision.

speechtext: Only on questions of law.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext:
Only on questions of law, yes. I say that what the manufacturers are enforcing is a private code of law. My hon. friend, if he likes, can discuss that point a little later.
Surely it follows, in any event, that this parliament cannot allow private manufacturers to establish a code of law from which there is no appeal either by the retailer or, what is more important, by the consumer. This, Mr. Speaker, seems to me to be the issue the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) put before us yesterday when he was referring to the principle upon which the MacQuarrie committee based its conclusion that resale price maintenance should be forbidden. As reported at page 2092 of Hansard he said this:
That the practice of resale price maintenance establishes a private system of law under which the business of a non-conforming retailer or of a retailer who is merely believed to be non-conforming may be seriously prejudiced without that retailer having any recourse to the courts of justice.
I want to press that point just one step further and say that in reality that is the real issue in connection with this legislation now before us.

Combines Investigation Act
The recent hearings before the parliamentary committee had more than passing significance to the people of Canada. That is obvious from the manner in which the proceedings have been quoted. No one appearing on behalf of those opposed to this bill supported free enterprise which, under other circumstances, they so loudly acclaim. On the contrary, manufacturers demanded not only the right but the support of this parliament- because if we now did not do anything in regard to legislation, it would go all across the country that we were more or less in favour of resale price maintenance-for their own private controls over segments of the Canadian economy.
I want to say at once that I can understand the attitude of many of the retailers and the organizations representing them which appeared before the committee. They remember the disastrous experiences in the 1930's when business was stagnant and when price cutting was quite prevalent. They had-perhaps I should say "they have"-good reason to fear a similar situation; but it is certain that if a similar situation occurred, price maintenance by private interests could not be enforced. It could not be enforced in the 1930's. It could not be enforced under similar circumstances should they arrive again in 1954 or 1960. It seems to me that they advance an argument which is quite unsound. Indeed, rival manufacturers would do exactly as they did in the 1930's, namely, compete with each other for the small amount of business retail merchants were likely to give them.
Thus, in reality, price maintenance as a protection in such circumstances seems to me to be quite useless. It may be true that price maintenance does not affect a large range of retail goods, with the exception perhaps of druggists' supplies.
In this connection, may I say that at page 137 of the proceedings of the committee, Mr. J. W. Preston, secretary-manager of the Canadian Pharmaceutical Association, was examined by Mr. Phelan. Mr. Phelan quoted an item from the association publication, in its issue of November 1, which said this:
From the time the speech from the throne was published and the newspaper stories started to appear, every druggist in Canada could see the disastrous results of any legislation for him: over 60 per cent of his volume is done on price-maintained products.
With that statement in this journal Mr. Preston substantially agreed. In his brief Mr. Preston gave some idea of how widespread the practice was. It was so widespread, indeed, that I think one might say that, as far as this particular type of business is concerned, the retail merchant is no longer an

independent retail merchant but that he is merely an agent for certain manufacturers.

Mr. Preston said this:
It is our contention that the principle of resale price maintenance is so woven into the fabric of our economy that any move to declare the practice illegal should not be made hastily, nor without scientific investigation.
We have had a number of investigations. And what did Mr. Preston say-that the retailer was the principal consideration in this respect? No, as a matter of fact he said that the protection of the manufacturer was the basic purpose of price maintenance-not the retailer, but the manufacturer. Examples were given at page 139 of the official evidence that increased profit margins on certain proprietary medicines had been announced and had been put into effect. From the evidence on these pages it would appear that druggists, as I have already said, have become very largely the agents of manufacturers.
Now I want to say immediately that I can understand the position taken by many of the local druggists who have approached their members of parliament and asked them to oppose this legislation. I have no doubt all members of parliament have been approached by some of the retail druggists in the country. These druggists quite often operate in small local communities where they meet a real community need and perform a useful and desirable service. They are afraid that if resale price maintenance is made unlawful, they will not be able to compete with large organizations in the large centres who sell through catalogues or chain organizations, and who buy in large quantities. There is no question that this has prompted many of the representations made to members of parliament.
As I said when reference of this matter to the committee was under discussion in the house, the bill should contain some provisions to prevent unfair competition. The MacQuarrie report itself draws attention to the unfair practice of advertising what are sometimes known as loss leaders. My hon. friend from Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) referred to this at some length this morning. The MacQuarrie report states, in this connection:
Resale price maintenance, by prohibiting any normal price reduction, affords an effective protection against loss leaders in the field of price-maintained goods. However, the committee does not think that to withdraw from the retailer the right to make any price reduction is a satisfactory way of preventing unfair and excessive pricecutting. We are of the opinion that more direct and desirable weapons can be found to curb loss leaders.
