subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house rose for lunch I was saying that we regretted that the bill did not include some provision to give some protection to the retailer in regard to matters I was talking about, namely, price cutting, loss leadership and so on. According to the transcript of evidence of proceedings before the committee the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) moved the following motion:
1. That no dealer shall sell or offer for sale directly or indirectly any commodity at a price less than 5 per cent above cost.
Then the motion provided exceptions in the case of sales of damaged goods, goods sold for charitable purposes or by relief agencies, perishable merchandise, goods sold in clearance sales or as bankrupt stock; and the cost was defined as the invoice cost to a bona fide dealer or the replacement cost; and so on. I am not at all sure that the 5 per cent is the percentage that should be included, but the idea behind that motion was one that I think deserved more consideration than it received and some such provision might well be included in this legislation.
As the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) said this morning, there is legislation concerning this practice in some 45 of the 48 states of the United States. Evidence in this regard may be found at page 688 where Mr. Phelan was examining Mr. Leach, as hon. members who were on the committee will remember. 1 quote from that page:
Q. Mr. Leach, you spoke about the fair trade law in the United States; would you be good enough, if
Combines Investigation Act you can, to outline to us what it is, how it works in the United States, and so on?
A. To the best of my knowledge, as I think I did explain earlier-I will try to be as brief as I can- the manufacturer submits his catalogue of prices to the state fair trade board, whatever it is called; that board approves of those prices if they feel they are right and then it issues a certificate and puts its O.K. on it and- says that is your price. You will go to the retailer and he signs a contract that he will sell at that price.
After a little further explanation there is another question and answer as follows:
Q. Now, in the United States, does that eliminate the question of the loss leader? I take it it does.
A. In cases where the retailer actually signs.
Q. But here in Canada do you think this would be an effective answer to the threat of the loss leader?
A. Most effective.
Much depends on the intent and spirit of the legislation under which such a provision operates and the board under which it would operate. In some states the legislation and the personnel of the board are such that it has not as much effect as we would desire it to have under our legislation. I have been reading some articles dealing with this provision in the United States and they point out that in many states, particularly California, it has had an effect the opposite of that which was originally intended. As a rule the legislation provides purely for voluntary agreements; there are no compulsory features and no penalties. Our legislation should be a part of and in the spirit of the Combines Investigation Act. Otherwise the cure might indeed be worse than the disease. I think we should be most careful about what we de in that direction.
Another practice which should be scrutinized and as far as possible banned is the giving of different rates of discount to large and small retailers. Mr. McGregor in his evidence gave examples of how this operates obviously against the small merchant and the consumer. He pointed out that under resale price maintenance this might very well tend to keep prices up because inducements offered to buy in larger quantities were not to benefit the consumers but to maintain larger margins and bigger profits. That was the evidence placed before the committee.
I would point out that in connection with the marketing of wheat under the government board and our legislation it does not matter whether one buys a bushel or one million bushels, the price per unit is exactly the same. In my own province of Saskatchewan the same thing applies to the fur marketing board. A man who has a few pelts sends them down to the marketing agency and he gets exactly the same price per pelt for the same grade as the producer who sends in, one thousand pelts. In other

Combines Investigation Act words, the unit cost to the retailer should be the same, instead of having these differentials which are brought about by means of discounts.
It was brought out in the evidence that the manufacturer did everything in his power to persuade merchants to maintain the agreed resale prices. This morning an hon,. member raised the question of a lawsuit in Montreal. I have only a very hazy idea of that lawsuit, but my understanding is that an effort was made to obtain an injunction to prevent a large wholesale drug firm from refusing to supply a retail merchant. It had nothing to do with the community; it was purely a matter between a retailer and manufacturer. What was actually happening was that a druggist wished to again get supplies on the basis of maintaining the resale price. Consequently it has no bearing on the discussion that we are having at the present time nor does it take away in any respect from my argument that what is really happening in Canada is that the manufacturers are taking to themselves the power to impose their own code of law and their own penalties in connection with the enforcement of that code. On the contrary it reinforces it.
In its report the parliamentary committee stated that it did not think that under present conditions there was any likelihood of any powerful retailing interests engaging in a policy of selling goods at unreasonably low prices for the purpose of destroying the independent retailer.
As a matter of fact, as the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) pointed out yesterday, we have in section 498A of our Criminal Code a provision which, if vigorously enforced and if the evidence could be obtained, would prevent that kind of discrimination. This section has been placed on the record already by the minister and by the hon. member for Kamloops. Therefore since my time is limited I shall omit placing it on the record again. But this provision in the Criminal Code, 498A, does not meet the point made by the MacQuarrie committee with regard to loss leaders, nor does it obviate the necessity for a provision similar to that moved by the hon. member for Spadina or, as I have said, the kind of provision that in the light of our circumstances will provide the same public control as some legislatures attempted to institute in the interests of the consumers and failed to do in many of the states of the United States.
My criticism of the report of the committee therefore is that it did not recommend legislation of this description. I believe if the bill is passed the combines commissioner should be asked to draft a suitable clause for


presentation to the house early in the next session of parliament. I believe that during the recess further consideration should be given to this matter. It is true, as the committee states, that there is not much present danger of loss leaders menacing the small merchant when the economy is as buoyant as it is at the present time and we are in a period of inflated price levels.
The hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) made much this morning of the representations made by Mr. Bengough on behalf of the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada, but what he actually did of course was to quote from their brief various paragraphs in which Mr. Bengough argued pro and con. But the meat of the brief, as usual of course, can be found in the recommendations contained therein which make a very material difference to my hon. friend's argument. Let me put on the record what the recommendations were. They are found at page 382. Perhaps I should read the preceding paragraphs, although it will be a little long. They read as follows:
What we should all be concerned about at this time is how to protect the individual whether he be consumer or merchant, distributor or manufacturer, worker or employer in a free economy. At the same time we must remember that a free economy does not exist because of some law; it exists1 because of the private arrangements, agreements, alliances, organizations and the whole welter of checks and balances which serve to offset any possibility of one group dominating it completely.
There are those who fear the domination of the economy by the state. Whatever grounds they may have for such alarm, it must be noted that the state already has a hand in the economy. Your committee is asked to consider what further hand the state shall take in the economy. What appears most important is not whether the state shall play a part in the economy or whether the economy will remain free if it does, but what part the state shall play; and whether the state shall play a negative and confusing role or a positive one.
While we would not recommend the repeal of the Combines Investigation Act, we believe that the negative approach of this type of legislation and administrative practice is unlikely to ever have very substantial influences upon consumer prices or to provide very effective means for reducing the private alliances that restrict the free flow of goods and services in a free economy.
What he is saying there is that there are restrictive alliances that do prevent the operation of a free economy and that '*something else than preventive legislation should be undertaken. He goes on to say:
We believe, on the other hand, that your committee should recommend positive measures for dealing with restrictive practices in our economy and in so doing provide parliament with suggestions for immediate action against inflation and rising consumer prices. Rather than say that a manufacturer may not make an arrangement to protect the price of his goods and thereby, presumably, his business, it would seem much more practical to suggest that the relationshiDS between suppliers

and distributors should be subject to broad social regulation thereby providing for the protection of both along with the consumer.
We suggest that your committee recommend the creation of a consumers price control board which will have power to deal with all aspects of this problem of resale price maintenance as well as with consumer prices generally. We make this recommendation to you because we believe that it would provide for a positive approach to the problem of restrictive practices in the economy and at the same time for a sensible and immediate attack on rising consumer prices in all lines.
Parliament has already granted the power to the government to deal with prices. Your committee, in our opinion should recommend that action be reserved along the negative lines of amending the Combines Investigation Act and rather that immediate positive action be taken through a consumers price control board to free the whole economy from restrictive price practices whether these arise as the result of agreements or arrangements or simply from the customs of the trade.
If you read that you see what Mr. Ben-gough was really asking for. He was really asking for some control of the economy and that that control should be exercised through powers given to a board representing the consumers of this country. That puts a very different light on the brief than the isolated quotations which my hon. friend put on the record this morning. We think this is a suggestion which is more worthy of consideration than any other, and much more indeed than the committee seemed to give it. Mention of the trades and labour congress reminds me that an argument sometimes used to support resale price maintenance is that farmers and labour maintain the prices of agricultural products and of wage levels. These of course are analogies which do not bear examination. Prices of farm goods are set not by any private arrangement but by public authority-

Mr. Speaker, at the outset I should like to review briefly some facts concerning the bill that is now before the house, and particularly the background which led up to the bill. In the first place, the government appointed the MacQuarrie committee in June, 1950, to undertake the study of existing combine legislation. In early September, 1951, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) requested from the committee an early report on resale price maintenance. This report, while it was designated as interim, was such only in the sense that the entire report on the combines was not completed. I think the Minister of Justice has quite fully established this fact, and I take it therefore that as far as resale price maintenance is concerned the MacQuarrie committee report was final and complete.
The second fact is this. The MacQuarrie committee in its report dated October 1, 1951, recommended legislation designed to prohibit the practice of resale price maintenance. They also recommended that the legislation to make it an offence for manufacturers to refuse to supply retailers with goods on the ground that these retailers had cut prices be enacted. The third fact is as follows: It has been established quite amply, I suggest, that the government accepted the MacQuarrie committee's recommendation. The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) announced in the speech from the throne at the opening of this present session that legislation to carry out the recommendation would be introduced during the present session. Later on it was announced by the government that a joint parliamentary committee would be set up to deal with the recommendation of the MacQuarrie committee.
The Minister of Justice gave as his reason for the committee the fact that representations had been received from manufacturers and retailers urging the government to hear their views before proceeding to have parliament enact any legislation. If there is any

criticism on this point-and I think there is- it is that the government did not get the committee under way as soon as they could have done, and as soon as it was necessary. Had the committee been set up earlier in the session, then perhaps it would have been possible to hear a great deal more evidence than was heard in the comparatively short time that it sat. I think that 16 sittings of the committee to hear 42 briefs and to scan and consider a large volume of wires and letters would hardly be enough time to give the kind of consideration that ought to have been given to expect hon. members to reach sound conclusions as to the various arguments that were put forward on all sides. In my judgment neither was there time for the government and the supporters of the bill completely to justify the legislation which the government has decided to adopt.
The fourth fact is this. As a consequence of the committee's deliberations at least four facts have been established so far as my thinking is concerned. I would like to set them out briefly at this point. The first is: The MacQuarrie committee apparently did not accumulate statistical evidence that would establish that under resale price maintenance Canadian consumers were being harmed. As far as I can gather from the evidence-and I must say here that I was not a member of the committee-the approach seemed to be more from the standpoint of principle than from detailed evidence.
Now, the second of these four facts that were established by the committee's deliberations is this. None of the trade associations which appeared before the parliamentary committee could go beyond expressing their opinion on the subject. I stress that word "opinion." It is true that certain statistical information was presented but it was found impossible, on the basis of what was before the committee, to make a proper comparison between the resale prices on price-maintained goods and, those of comparable nonprice-maintained goods. The argument was frequently advanced during the sittings of the committee that, generally speaking, maintained prices were lower than non-maintained prices. This basis was, in fact, not proven because the committee did not take the time to accumulate information upon which a proper comparison could be made. I think the opposition has some legitimate criticism to make on this score, although the Minister of Justice (Mr. Gar son) did present considerable evidence to show that at least in other countries the endi price of price-maintained goods was somewhat higher than the end price of non-price-maintained goods.
Combines Investigation Act No real effort was made, however, to establish the facts of the situation right here in Canada, and I think that is regrettable.
The member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) has complained that the committee actually choked off attempts by the opposition members of the committee to gather information which would establish, one way or the other, what the effect of resale price maintenance really is. The hon. member now interpolates that it was the government that choked off those attempts. If the hon. member's statements are correct, then the government is to be severely criticized for not having taken the time or made the effort to establish the facts.
Fact No. 3, which has emerged as a result of the sittings of the committee, is that spokesmen of certain trade organizations argued that price maintenance was designed for the protection of the retailer; others were perfectly frank in asserting it was designed to protect the manufacturer. What studies I have been able to give this particular problem, together with the evidence submitted by the Minister of Justice in his submission last evening, has led me to the conclusion that the principal purpose of resale price maintenance has been to protect the manufacturer. I cannot escape that conclusion. I confess that I may be wrong, but thus far my studies have led me to that conclusion.
Fact No. 4 is that the percentage of price maintained goods found in any store varies a great deal. In a grocery store, for example, less than one per cent of the goods are price maintained. Sixty per cent or more of the goods in drugs stores are price maintained. Jewelry, silverware and watches which make up the bulk of the goods in any jewelry store are price maintained to approximately 90 per cent. Taking these facts into consideration, and adding to them the evidence of the Minister of Justice which I thought was well documented and well supported, I have concluded that if resale price maintenance were prohibited it would not unduly affect the retailers as a whole. I have concluded too, Mr. Speaker, that it would not affect very greatly the retailers whose percentage of price maintained' goods is very low. In fact, I think it is self-evident that it would not.
It must be remembered, of course, that most retailers' establishments do handle a small volume of price maintained goods. On the other hand, if the bulk of the retailer's goods is price maintained, as long as that practice is continued I must conclude that the retailer is at the mercy of the manufacturer, who exercises the power to discontinue his supplies if he should cut prices by even- the smallest amount. It is our opinion that no retailer should be submitted to a system of

Combines Investigation Act private law from which there is no appeal to any court in the land. If I recall correctly the British report on resale price maintenance did condemn the practice on that ground1.
Those are the four facts which I believe did emerge crystal clear as a result of the deliberations of the committee. I should like to continue with my general comment. It was significant to me that most manufacturers did deny that there had been rigid enforcement of resale price maintenance. The jewelry people, for example, even went so far as to create the impression that there was no enforcement at all. If that is true, then one has to ask, Why do they display such concern over the abolition of the practice? Most manufacturers stressed the value to the public of branded goods. They argued during the sittings of the committee that the only way by which branded names and branded goods could be continued with assurance of quality was through the maintenance of price. Now, sir, I sought diligently for the facts which would establish the validity of that argument in my mind, but I must confess I could not find them. Consequently, I am forced to conclude that the manufacturers' contention in this regard is at least highly questionable.
I must admit thai anyone would find it extremely difficult to -establish beyond question that resale price maintenance is on the one hand good or, on the other, evil. At least, that is the way it appears to me on the basis of the evidence that is available. I cannot overlook, however, that it is a growing practice. Let me emphasize that, that it is a growing practice. It seemed to me the Minister of Justice established that fact beyond any question last night.
I should like to refer to the evidence of Mr. F. A. McGregor, the former combines commissioner. If I recall correctly, his evidence was heard on November 28, and I shall read a paragraph to emphasize the importance of that point I have just made, that the practice of resale price maintenance is growing. Mr. McGregor says, at page 390 of the committee's proceedings:
The extension of the practice in recent years has been alarming. If it continues it will not be long before price control by manufacturers will become the rule in the distributive trade and price competition the exception, as far as branded goods are concerned. Indeed in some trades the practice has already become so general that practically none of these goods can be reduced in price without the authorization of the manufacturer. The development of such a system may be very enterprising on the part of the dealers and manufacturers, but it can hardly be described as "free enterprise" in the meaning of that term which used to be commonly accepted. Nor can it be said to have any rightful part in a competitive system, which has been recognized by parliament as a basic element in our


whole economy. The undoubted right of the public to the safeguard afforded by price competition is being supplanted to this extent and in these broadening areas, by the questionable right of manufacturers and dealers to prevent price competition in the wholesale and retail selling of their particular products. If the vital element of price competition is removed from a competitive system, what you have left is not a competitive system at all, but a price-controlled system-with prices controlled by manufacturers. In the case of resale price maintenance it is control by the manufacturers with ready acquiescence and indeed urgent advocacy on the part of a very large proportion of the dealers, whose interests it is primarily designed to protect. The minority of dealers who would prefer to maintain their independence and determine their own selling prices have no alternative but to fall in line.
I do not believe we can disregard the evidence of a man of such broad experience as Mr. McGregor has had. It has already been argued that he is a theorist, and therefore should be discounted. Let me say this, Mr. Speaker: On many occasions in this house I have heard this man quoted as if he were the most practical man in the field of combine legislation, and that argument was not confined to the government side of the house.
It appears to us that, the more and more firms adopt the device of resale price maintenance, the evil, if it can be called an evil, is bound to become apparent as time goes on, and especially in the light of the fact that manufacturers are put in such a strong position the retailers will no longer be free to carry on in any capacity other than as agents of manufacturers. My own judgment tells me that is not good. Such a contingency as that would be very harmful, both to the retailers themselves and to consumers generally. In my judgment this important matter cannot be considered properly unless one takes a long-range view, and not just a short-range view. It is very largely on that long-range view of what this thing could become that we in this group take our position.
As a matter of principle, we cannot agree that manufacturers should be allowed to exercise a law of their own. They should never be in a position to put retailers out of business to suit their whims, nor to dictate resale prices, especially when the retailer or consumer who may be deprived of these goods through the action of the manufacturer cannot go to the courts to secure justice. We would have to oppose resale price maintenance on this ground, even if no other reasons existed iat all.
Most manufacturers indicated some fear that the removal of resale price maintenance would immediately result in widespread use of the loss-leader practice. Much has been said about that matter already, and for that reason I do not intend to go into it at any length. The manufacturers assumed that

branded goods would be the first affected; and they said that large stores would likely indulge in the practice in order to squeeze out weaker opposition. It is significant, Mr. Speaker-and I should like to mention this- that the large stores opposed resale price maintenance. That is a significant fact. However, I think the Minister of Justice, in his case last evening, fairly well disposed of any fears that the manufacturers have. He showed that predatory price-cutting tactics are not only against the public interest but are also contrary to section 498A of the Criminal Code. It appears to me that the federal government has authority to take action against the practice of loss leader if that practice begins, in any way, to endanger the legitimate competition that exists or should exist between retailers. I should caution the government, of course, at this time that they will have to be on their guard against predatory price cutting by large concerns especially if, in the days ahead, we slide into a buyer's market. We have not been in one for a good many years, but it is possible that we could get into a buyer's market. More settled conditions throughout the world could quickly bring us into such a market.
In my judgment the Criminal Code should be invoked wherever and whenever necessary to protect the small merchants. If I thought that this legislation would endanger the position of the small retailers throughout this country, I would do my best to hold the bill over until a full investigation of all the evidence could be made, or I would do my best to defeat it. I should like to see made crystal clear, one way or the other, exactly what effect it will have upon the small retailers. We are much concerned about keeping retail merchants everywhere in Canada in a strong and happy position. It seems to me that, in a house like this, nobody needs to emphasize, any more than has been done, the important place that the retail merchant holds in our economy; it is an exceedingly important place. Without strong and secure retail merchants in our country we could not carry on under what is called a free economy. That is one of the reasons why we spend so much time in trying to get the government to lay down policies under which Canada can be assured a balanced economy in which there will always be effective purchasing power in the pockets of consumers sufficient to enable them to buy all of the goods and services available for sale, if they want them.
Under the kind of balanced economy we Social Crediters advocate, we think the position of the retailers would constantly be a happy and prosperous one, especially if the
Combines Investigation Act practice of predatory price cutting is prosecuted with vigour under the Combines Investigation Act and the Criminal Code, and if conditions are established wherein fair competition can be assured. We in this parliament must be sure that the small merchants and druggists of this country are not adversely affected by this legislation or by anything that we do. If, by the time of the next session of parliament, it appears that there are or will be injustices to the independent merchants as a result of what we are doing- that is, through the application of the terms of this bill-then we must be ready to amend *the act to remove the injustices or even to repeal the act.
We are thinking also of the consumer generally, Mr. Speaker. The consumer has, for too long, been the forgotten man; and it is high time that something was done for him. It is our opinion that the passing of this bill will help the consumers of Canada directly and perhaps also indirectly. But when I say that, I want it understood, Mr. Speaker, that we do not look upon the abolition of resale price maintenance as any substitute for a vigorous program of action by the government to bring down the high cost of living. I am of the opinion that the unusual circumstances surrounding the birth of this bill indicate that the government wants the people to think that it is really going out to do battle for a lower general consumer price level. We are not being fooled by that, by any means, if that really is what the government wants the people to believe. We shall continue in our efforts to press the government to take the earliest possible action to relieve the consuming public from the present unnecessarily high living costs.
I think that one of the strongest arguments put forward by the Minister of Justice in his case last night for the bill was that resale price maintenance has made it difficult to detect a manufacturers' combine that may be operating behind the practice. I think he referred to that matter at page 15 of his submission, if I remember correctly. It therefore seems to me that to get this out of the way ought to make possible more efficient, successful and vigorous administration of the Combines Investigation Act. In our judgment, this alone would be of great good to the consumers of Canada.
I should now like to say by way of conclusion, Mr. Speaker-I do not want to prolong the debate, by any means-that we find that we shall have to oppose the amendment. We think that it would be wise to pass the bill now, to give it a trial and to see what

Combines Investigation Act it can do; and then, in the light of the experience which we gain, when we come back here at the next session I think we could take whatever action would be necessary to see that justice is meted out to all sections of our society.

speechtext:
My felicitations, Mr. Speaker, are not on the contribution that my hon. friend's speech made to this debate but rather to the debate we are going to have tomorrow on procedure, because his speech is the best argument I have ever heard for a further limitation on the time of speeches in the house.
I should like to start off by reminding hon. members that the principal purpose of this legislation now before the house is to further strengthen the Combines Investigation Act. We on this continent are all fairly familiar with the history and the story of combines legislation. With the great growth of industrial power in the United States, combines, trusts and cartels, formed by powerful groups of selfish people in order to exploit the consumer to the utmost, began to be established. President Teddy Roosevelt around the turn of the century established the first anti-combine legislation. The vicious practice of combines spread to this country and we were the second country in the world to establish, in 1925, under a Liberal government, anti-combine legislation. We have a good record with regard to the breaking up and the prosecution of these illegal combines, monopolies and cartels; in fact, we have a record second to no other nation in the world. It is true last spring there was a delay in the publication of the milling report, between the time of the report by the commissioner and the presentation in the house, because of a difference of opinion with the


wartime prices and trade board, as to what undertakings they had given the millers under wartime price control.
But in all the records of the twenty-seven investigations of the combines investigators I would recall to the attention of hon. members that there are five reports which had never been published, five investigations made under the regime of the Bennett government. There was the combine in the manufacture of radio tubes in 1931, unpublished; the manufacturing of fruit baskets in Ontario in 1932, unpublished; the distribution of coal in eastern Canada, 1933, unpublished; the manufacture of rubber footwear in Canada, 1934, unpublished, and the sale of gasoline in Ontario, 1934, unpublished.
However, for fear anyone has any doubt about our record as against that of other nations in the world, let me say that our record is second to none in the world. This matter was shown by the debate on international cartels by the United Nations economic council last summer, at which I was present. The United States is first, we are second, and the next nation in the world having legislation anything like this is Sweden, and that country in 1946 passed legislation based on ours, then Britain in 1948, although as yet they have had no investigations under their act.
For fear I am being prejudiced, let us see what one of the great leaders in the Conservative party, the man said to have the finest and clearest mind in the party, Sir David Maxwell Fyfe, had to say. He published a book for the Tory party, on monopoly, in 1948, giving the British Conservative view on it, and especially referring to legislation that the Labour government was bringing forward against monopolies. He reviewed other countries' legislation on combines, and led off with the United States and then Canada. And at page 49 he said:
Other British dominions have passed laws against trade restraints though none are as complete or effective as the Canadian law.
This is surely a real tribute to Canadian Liberal legislation. However, despite our good law and competent staff, there has been the great difficulty in connection with prosecuting combines because of securing proof. These powerful, selfish and ruthless interests who form combines to rob the consumer do not do their deeds in the public light. As Mr. McGregor said, these deeds are done by stealth, but with effective legislation and staff they can be brought to light; and he has certainly done that. However, from the start, throughout, inquiries into restrictive practices in connection with combines has run this

Combines Investigation Act
thread of resale price maintenance, often the thread which held the whole evil web together.
The first inquiry was in 1926-27 into the druggists Proprietary Articles Trade Association, the P.A.T.A. At that time there were 167 drug manufacturers, 28 wholesale druggists and 2,734 retail druggists who got together to fix the price of all drug products. And that was done for the benefit of whom? Certainly it was not done for the benefit of the consumer! And it was Mr. McGregor who smashed that P.A.T.A. in 1927. But in most investigations since that time there has again run the thread of resale price maintenance. And if hon. members wish to read of the details then I would suggest that they read the evidence of Mr. McGregor at page 390, or the brief of the Canadian Congress of Labour at page 73. They will see how resale price maintenance was connected with these various combines. It was present in the drug combine in 1926, and the tobacco combine in 1927, as it is described at page 74. Then there was again in the dental supplies combine in 1947, and optical goods combine in 1948.
Then there was again in the bread-making combine in western Canada, when they even fixed the price of bread in 1948; and there was again in the match combine of 1950-and that was the worst of the lot.
Then, further evidence along this line was given, as has been pointed out by the Minister of Justice, in the report of the royal commission on prices who found the practice of price fixing increasingly affecting prices in Canada.
Then the MacQuarrie committee was established to study and recommend methods of strengthening the Combines Investigation Act. They drew specific attention to resale price maintenance as a restrictive business practice. And in this connection I would refer the house to the letter which they sent out to all manufacturers and trade associations which appears at page 250 of the proceedings of the committee, which drew special attention to the fact that they were going to make an investigation of resale price maintenance. Paragraph 6 of this letter states:
You may recall that the royal commission on prices in their examination of restrictive business practices gave particular attention to the practice of resale price maintenance and recommended that careful study be given to this problem from the viewpoint of its effect on price competition amongst wholesalers and retailers. In view of this the committee invites comments on this particular problem as well as on the Combines Investigation Act generally. In particular, the committee would appreciate receiving extended comments on the tentative conclusion of the royal commission on prices as to the effects of the practice upon the public interest. The matter is dealt with in Vol.
I, pages 27, 28 and 41, and Vol. II, pages 256 to 259 of the report of the royal commission on prices as published by the king's printer in 1949.
So those manufacturers who have said that they had no warning that the Mac-Quarrie committee were to deal with price fixing by manufacturers were certainly not speaking the truth.
The MacQuarrie committee made their interim report to the government on resale price maintenance. The government received it and accepted it and announced in the speech from the throne that it would have legislation to implement the recommendations of that committee.
There were many objections from manufacturers and retailers, who asked for further inquiry in a public forum. Then the government, as a consequence of these representations, set up the parliamentary committee to give these people an opportunity to state publicly their objections to this legislation which would do away with resale price maintenance.
Hon. members in this House of Commons will recall the attitude of the Tory party then. Their spokesman was the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker), and what he said can be found at page 667 of Hansard. Referring to the MacQuarrie committee he said:
That committee, composed of outstanding men, called upon all those affected, including consumers and manufacturers, to send in their briefs. Has not that committee for a year and a half importuned either directly by letter or indirectly through the press asking interested parties to produce evidence regarding resale price maintenance, a subject of more than academic interest to the members of that committee?
And then in the next column on the same page:
Is it to postpone action and procrastinate? . . . Why postpone and hold back the legislation? Why further delay?
And the very interesting thing about that speech was that it was a very powerful speech, when one listened to it. But when you read it the next morning in Hansard, away from the persuasive eloquence, you will find in it no indication whatever as to what his views are on resale price maintenance. If you remember that speech of the hon. member, you find in it nowhere any mention of where he stood in connection with price maintenance. In that respect it was similar to his speech on price control, where again he made a rousing speech but never even mentioned where he stood on price control.
Well, perhaps that is not so surprising, after all; because, after hearing the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) this
morning declare-and after all, he was

Combines Investigation Act speaking for his party-"We are not taking a strong position either for or against resale price maintenance"-I say, one can understand the position of the official opposition.
Of course we in the House of Commons are used to this shilly-shallying by the Tories. They twist and they turn, and they sit on the fence. We remember that they twisted and turned and skated all round the manpower situation last session. We remember that they turned sideways, and turned this way and that way on price controls, talking for them but voting against the C.C.F. motion for price controls. Then, this time they say they are neutral. They are neutral-how? They are neutral like the Irish in the last war, who picked sides. In this issue the Tories are neutral, neutral against the hard-pressed consumer of Canada and neutral for the price-fixing manufacturer.
And then what is the position of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew)? This is what he says as reported at page 753 of Hansard:
The government by its present action makes it clear that it does not intend to act upon the recommendations they bring forward.
Well, the legislation before us today shows that, as usual, he is wrong.
Now, when the committee was called I was elected chairman. And I wish to point this out again, in view of the comments of the hon. member for Kamloops this morning. I say I was unanimously elected chairman of the committee, and that the hon. member for Kamloops himself and the other Tories voted for me.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext:
The hon. member's memory is faulty, because he and all other members will recall that my election as chairman was carried unanimously. I remember because I was delighted to have his support. But though the member for Lake Centre said the government was stalling and delaying it was the hon. member and his friends who delayed and obstructed the proceedings of the committee, in calling for more and more repetitive evidence from provincial and local retailers. It was he who with a straight face suggested that the T. Eaton Company should come and produce all their records. I doubt whether even this large chamber would have held all those records, and it would have taken the members of the committee years to even thumb through them.
Finally, despite the fact that the hon. member for Lake Centre accused the government of stalling and delaying this legislation, we find it is the hon. member for Kamloops, on behalf of the Tory party, who now offers real delay by moving that this bill be postponed for six months. Today hon. members in this house can judge who is stalling and delaying.
When our committee convened, the clerk of the committee wrote to all those trade groups who had publicly stated that they had made representations before the MacQuarrie committee. He wrote to those who had written to the Minister of Justice asking for a further hearing. Through the press we gave an invitation to all groups interested to file briefs which would be studied by the committee. At first we said that we would print some of those briefs, but in the end we printed all the briefs, for the information of all members and the general public.
We decided as a matter of policy to hear further from certain groups who had raised points in their briefs requiring further explanation. We faced a problem which is faced by every committee of this house which sits on a matter of national concern, the fact that so many people want to come forward with briefs which are largely repetitious. So we decided that in the main we would hear national organizations, and would hear provincial or local organizations only when they dissented from the briefs submitted by their parent national organization. Because

we did not want to be accused of stalling and delaying we gave first preference to those who had asked for the committee to express their views against this legislation, the Retail Federation of Canada, the Canadian Manufacturers Association, the electrical manufacturers, the druggists, the jewelers, the beauty equipment manufacturers and the hardware people.
The groups which were for the legislation, the consumers, the housewives, the farmers, organized labour, very generously forbore demanding to be heard. They said they would stand on their briefs and on the evidence of Fred McGregor. They said that they would rather have legislation than be a party to stalling and delaying it. Because of these circumstances the press was filled with the story of those who were opposed to the legislation and as a result many people became utterly bewildered. The term resale price maintenance does not mean much to the man on the street. That was made quite clear by the lawyer for the hardware dealers who appeared before the committee. He said that as soon as he was appointed he went around to a lot of his friends and asked them how they felt about resale price maintenance and most of them said that they did not know what it was. Then he asked them how they felt about private price-fixing by the manufacturer and they were all against it. I think that is the attitude of the great majority of the people of Canada.
What is resale price maintenance? Resale price maintenance is the practice by which a large manufacturer tells the retailers at what price they must sell his goods so that all goods are sold at the same price by all retailers, big and small, efficient and inefficient, whether they sell for cash or whether they sell for credit. If they do not do that, then sanctions in some form are applied to bring them in line.
There is one interesting thing as far as the Combines Investigation Act is concerned. If the manufacturers get together in a back room and decide that such a retail price shall be the official price, that is obviously an illegal combine and it would be up to our efficient combines branch to commence proceedings against them. If all the retailers organized together, that would also be a combine. Because there would be more of them, it would be that much easier for our combines branch to find out. But if each manufacturer tells all his retailers at what price they are to sell, then it is easy for those manufacturers to get together informally without agreement and agree on this fixed price to the consumer. The effect on the
Combines Investigation Act consumer is the same, there is artificial fixing of prices at too high a level. That is really the case against resale price maintenance.
That is the case which was made against it in the British house. That is the case that was made against the great drug combine over there. The British have had some experience in this as this practice has developed to a much greater degree over there because of lack of legislation than in this country. There in many industries all the retailers have got together in a price fixing association. It was cases of that kind that brought about Lloyd Jacob's report; then a debate in the house; then a white paper announcing government policy against price maintenance and then a final debate in the house. I think perhaps the best evidence was given in the House of Commons by Sir Hartley Shawcross, who was then president of the board of trade, who read a letter which had been handed to him by a Conservative member of parliament. The letter reads: Dear Sir:
I am writing to ask your help and advice; what I want to know is, is it an offence to sell cheap? I bought some hand cream to retail at Is. 4d. a tube. After a while the price rose to Is. 8d. I did not raise my price. A woman bought a tube from me at Is. 4d. She had been sent in by the P.A.T. Association who reported me for not raising the price to Is. 8d. A man from the P.A.T.A. told me that unless I raised my price to Is. 8d. I would have my name placed on the P.A.T.A. stoplist and supplies would be stopped. My husband is a diabetic and unable to run my business. He is an ex-service man, 1914-18. Our seven sons served in the last war and some were wounded.
Then follows a comment which Sir Hartley Shawcross rightly considered to be inconsequential.
Needless to tell you that my husband, myself, and seven sons, and one daughter voted for you.
That is, voted Conservative.
That is the type of thing that was happening in Britain under more developed price fixing. When there were infringements of their private rules they withdrew all goods from a particular store. That is what they did in the case of this woman and they left her bankrupt against which she had no recourse at law. They also have a system of fines, they have a private code of law for those who offend against their rules, the sort of thing to which the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) referred to in his speech a little earlier.
Even here in Canada we have had organizations similar to the British P.A.T.A. We need constant vigilance to see that these evil practices are not started again. Despite the fact that we broke up the Canadian P.A.T.A., I should like to refer hon. members to the evidence given in the committee when the

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext:
In this bureau of commercial interests we have P.A.T.A. all over again fixing prices and mark-ups. This witness first said the bureau had no interest in prices or mark-ups and then six instances were placed on the record to show that they had publicly boasted of a very great interest. Mr. Preston was the editor of the magazine in which those articles had occurred. Mr. McGregor said that this practice is growing. In the case of the beauty equipment manufacturers, in 1945 less than half their goods were price-maintained, but now it is over 90 per cent. In the case of the electrical appliances, it is up to 80 per cent; drugs, 60 per cent; jewelry, from nothing to 90 per cent depending on the store; hardware, the percentage is quite small, just under 8 per cent.
The Canadian Retail Federation, which represents nationally all the group of retail merchant associations, appeared before the committee at three sessions. They admitted that their views were not unanimous. As a matter of fact Mr. Harris, their representative, was asked if they represented all retailers and he said they did not. Part of the question and the answer given on page 266 was as follows:
Do those members who do not agree with your position fall into any group or any category of retailers?
A. No. They constitute both large and small retailers. I do not know them by name.
Q. Are they a particular type of retailer, such as a department store, or just retailers?
A. No, they are just quite free-wheeling retailers.
They are the sort of real free enterprisers who have made business grow in Canada. All hon. members no doubt have received letters from retailers in their own ridings on this subject. I at the beginning of this committee hearing received just eight; six from druggists, one from a grocer and one from a hardware merchant. I have sent them all the proceedings of our committee. I knew of course of these panic letters which had been sent out by trade associations who create alarm now and again to justify their existence, but I was surprised to receive only eight letters as a

result. So I wrote confidential letters to quite a number of other retailers in my riding whom I knew very well, because these letters on account of the fear of reprisals have to be in confidence as were many of the letters submitted to our committee. I asked them if they had received these alarming trade association letters, and if so, why they had not written me in protest, as directed. The answers I received can be divided into about three groups. Some of the little retailers up the coast in my riding said they did not know what resale price maintenance was all about and so didn't bother writing me. The second group said they did not care, they were always getting these panicky letters but they sold their goods for the price they could get for them. However, the third and largest group-and this is a very interesting thing- wrote me and said that they did not bother writing because they did not believe that Louis St. Laurent and the Liberal party were going to sell the small man down the river.
The retail federation in their evidence expressed great fear that the little man was going to be squeezed out by banning manufacturer's price fixing. Yet the figures of the dominion bureau of statistics put on the record by the Minister of Justice show beyond question that the little man is the most efficient retailer in Canada. The large corporation has its large overhead, its inflexible regulations and its much heavier taxes, because the Liberal government has given the small man a break and encouraged him by lower taxes. Most little stores are not companies. The owner only pays his ordinary personal income tax. When they get larger they incorporate but even then they pay only 20 per cent corporation tax on profits up to $10,000, and personal income tax as well. But the big boys, the chain stores and department stores, pay over 51 per cent corporation taxes on their profits and then personal income tax as well when these profits are paid out as dividends. That is the break which this government and the Minister of Finance have given small enterprise in Canada.
Another interesting thing is that in most retail businesses only a fraction of their trade is resale price maintained. The best example is the grocery stores. Less than one per cent of the goods in the ordinary food store are price maintained, and where are there more little men in business than in the food stores? Where are there better merchandising techniques than in the modern food store, and where is the mark-up less? They are an example of what real free trade can mean. If the little retailers are more efficient why are they worried? The reason they are worried is because of the big discounts given by
Combines Investigation Act manufacturers to large retailers. Those manufacturers who came before our committee shedding crocodile tears over the little retailers have the solution right in their hands, the solution suggested by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. Let them set prices not to the consumer but to the retailer. If they sell at the same price to the big man and the little man, as does the wheat board, for example, then the little man can make the most of his extra efficiency. The remedy is in their own hands.
Then of course there was fear expressed about loss leaders. It was very interesting that loss leaders were never exactly defined for the committee by any of the witnesses before us. They were variously defined as less than the laid-down cost, less than cost plus overhead, less than cost plus the full mark-up, but one thing was established, namely, that loss leaders are the product of resale price maintenance in the great bulk of the goods on the market. The jewelers' association spokesman came before the committee and slapped down twenty-five pages of bargains out of one issue of the Toronto Star to show that there was ample opportunity for competition in the field which is not resale price-maintained, a great argument to the consumers for free trade. It is only when a uniform manufacturers' fixed price across the country is dropped by one retailer that it suddenly appears because of its uniqueness as a very attractive bargain and so becomes a loss leader.
The head of the retail federation said it was not ethical to use the profits on the sale of other goods to hammer down the price of one particular price maintained product. The question arises of course: What is the reward for efficiency? With our retailers, as with everything else, we have very efficient retailers, retailers of average efficiency and some who are not so efficient. With fixed prices how can the efficient retailer pass on to his consumers the advantage of his efficiency? That question was asked of the representative of the Canadian Manufacturers Association, and his answer, to be found at page 577 of the proceedings of the committee, was as follows:
If you are maintaining a price, as long as you do maintain that price, then the retailer can neither pass along to the consumer the benefits of his efficiency or the penalties of his inefficiency.
The hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Jutras) asked the same question of the head of the retail federation. He wanted to know how the efficient retailer can pass on to his consumers the benefits of his efficiency. The head of the retail federation answered in

Combines Investigation Act this fashion, as found at page 268 of the proceedings of the committee:
Very easily indeed, on the items which are not price-maintained. He is going to give the people that benefit.
It is apparently unethical to take profits from other lines and lower prices on resale price maintained lines. That is loss leader -ing according to the retail federation. But it is apparently quite ethical to take the excess profits of the efficient merchant under resale price maintenance and then, according to the head of the retail federation, lower the prices of those goods which are competing openly on the market without price fixing. Very curious ethics!
There was an argument advanced by one C.C.F. member-and he did not speak for his party-and by the Tory members that resale price maintenance, price-fixing by manufacturers, is just the same thing as labour unions getting together and establishing a flat rate of wages, or the same as the farm support boards setting floor prices for agricultural products. I say on behalf of the Liberal party first of all that the Liberal party has never regarded labour as a commodity to be priced like a bag of sugar or a bag of potatoes. The second thing is that the labour employer, the buyer of the service, and the labour union, the seller of the service, come face to face under government legislation-, approved either by parliament or by the legislatures where the public has an interest, and agree on the price which they are going to pay and receive for labour. If they cannot agree then we have, again through public legislation, the process of conciliation and arbitration. The same is true with farm boards where the government, whether it be the federal government or a provincial government, sets up the boards for the public, and on each of them the consumer has representation. But the manufacturer fixing prices in the back room gives the consumer no representation. If there is going to be any price fixing done, then, as the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar said, it should be done under public legislation by the government and not by the manufacturers in back rooms.
The next point raised was the rigidity of resale price maintenance. Of course the funny thing is that resale price maintenance, which is so important to some manufacturers, was shown to us to be certainly not rigid. Let me give you some evidence. The electrical manufacturers said there was no control on the value of trade-ins and therefore the retailer who wants to give a fictitiously high value for a trade-in can do so. Seventy-five per cent of the retail electrical trade accepts

trade-ins and so by giving high trade-in values they effectively lower the manufacturer's fixed price to the consumer. At page 325 of the proceedings of the committee Mr. Longestaff of the electrical manufacturers said:
If you went into any retailer and wanted to buy an appliance he would give you 10 per cent or 15 per cent off if you did not tell anybody.

The manager of the Canadian Jewellers Association said the same thing. At page 682 of the proceedings of the committee he said:
I think when a customer goes into a store the retailer will make his own arrangements with him; and if the customer says: "I want my cash discount," I think the average retailer would give it to him and not turn him away.
A little farther on he said:
If you were my cash customer and you said:	"I
want my 6 per cent cash discount," I would say that as a retailer I would be terribly stupid if I did not give it to you in spite of price maintenance. The only harm in price cutting is in the advertising of it.
I want to speak on behalf of the ordinary Canadian purchaser. We have been reared not to barter like Arabs in eastern bazaars but to go to the store and pay the price which is shown. What advantage is it to that decent person to know that under this present system of price maintenance, less honourable people can go to a jeweler and haggle and get 10 or 15 per cent reduction on resale price-maintained goods or 5 or 6 per cent discount for cash "as long as nobody knows". I want to speak too for the honest merchant who, having a contract to fix prices with the manufacturer, does not chisel by giving discounts to demanding customers "as long as nobody knows about it". That leads us to this very interesting point about Eaton's brief. We had before the committee Mr. Hougham, whom the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) has well described as one of the ablest witnesses to appear before the committee. When asked why Eaton's had submitted such a brief he said, as recorded at page 767 of the proceedings of the committee:
... I would think one of the reasons they are opposed to resale price maintenance is that it is not effective, it is not completely effective. In other words, in order that they might be protected themselves from price competition they would have to, and do, employ a very considerable shopping force to watch their competitors to see

that their competitors' prices are comparable with tneirs, and for that reason they do not want to be tied to a contract which binds them but does not effectively bind their competitors.
You could not go into these big stores and haggle over resale price maintenance and get a discount "provided nobody was looking." Yet these stores must compete against those who, while subscribing to price fixing, will do this, "provided nobody is looking."
The major effects of this legislation will be to strengthen the Combines Investigation Act. That is the opinion of both the past and present combines commissioners. There are two secondary effects-and I say they are secondary effects-on the cost of living. One is immediate. Free competition in this country will undoubtedly reduce some of these resale price-maintained prices, which are unduly high. It was defended of course in the committee on the ground that the resale price maintenance percentage mark-up is lower than on free trade goods. Of course one other thing was pointed out, namely, that on resale price-maintained goods the manufacturer does the advertising. In other goods the retailer has to do the advertising, and so obviously should get a bigger mark-up. But it is not percentage mark-ups that are important to the consumer; it is the price he pays. It was pointed out by many witnesses that accurate comparisons are [DOT] difficult; in the vast field of consumer goods in Canada there are so many varying stores, varying conditions of sale and varying qualities. We have, however, three good comparisons. The first one is that of the United States. It was pointed out that in the United States of America there are three free trade states and forty-five states where price maintenance is the law and so identical goods are sold under both conditions. That has been dealt with already. A very fine article appeared in the American magazine Fortune, which is not the voice of big business, but it is certainly the mirror of big business in the United States. In the issue of January, 1949, which is in the library, there was a leading article entitled: "The Not-so-fair-trade-laws." It points out, as stated by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) that a comparison between Maryland and Washington, a free trade state and a nonfree trade state, showed that of 117 branded drug items 35 per cent cost about one-third less in Washington than in Maryland; 38 about a quarter less; and 29 about one-seventh less. In the druggists' own brief at page 543 they compare price-fixed Kansas and free-trade Missouri. They show Phillips' milk of magnesia, 21 cents in Missouri, 49 cents in-Kansas; Zonite, 59 cents in Missouri, 79 cents
Combines Investigation Act in Kansas; Murine, 34 cents in Missouri, 49 cents in Kansas; Bromo-Seltzer, 39 cents in Missouri, 57 cents in Kansas; Anacin, 89 cents in Missouri, 98 cents in Kansas. They point out that as a result of that the Kansas housewives, veterans and consumer organizations are on the march. Well they might be!
The second example is right here in Canada. The province of Newfoundland, before union, did not enjoy the blessing of resale price maintenance, but when they came into union they got it. And as the Newfoundland co-operative brief pointed out, the prices in every line except cars rose immediately when resale price maintenance was applied to Newfoundland and so they had a royal commission on this matter. The hon. member for Burin-Burgeo (Mr. Carter), and I hope the members of the Conservative party from St. John's as well, will speak further on this. Let me give you one example. The ordinary little ignition battery used by fishermen there before union cost the retailer 45J cents landed, and he sold it for 60 cents. After union it cost him a cent more, 46J cents, but resale price maintenance, this great benefit to the consumer, got the price up to 80 cents. That is quite a price to pay for resale price maintenance.

On this question, the greatest authority In Canada on combines, the man who has beaten them, came before this committee and said that the abolition of resale price maintenance will do just that. That man of course is Mr. McGregor, who was combines commissioner for 25 years. He was requested by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) at page 670 of Hansard as follows:
Let us bring in Mr. McGregor because I am sure that if his lips are unbridled, if he comes In unhobbled by any consideration other than to help the committee, he will make some revelations that will be most interesting and I am sure most helpful in suggesting effective amendments to the net.

He is the number one man in this business if we want to get at the facts.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure the house has welcomed the relaxation provided by the matinee performance which has just been concluded. It was an extraordinary histrionic performance. It will not be hard for those who have any claim to open minds on this subject to realize, after the performance we have just witnessed, how utterly hopeless it was in that parliamentary committee to try to obtain a fair hearing for both sides of the question. We have had a great conglomeration of distorted references to evidence, abuse of witnesses, etc., all of which is in keeping with the sort of thing we witnessed in that committee day in and day out at the hands of the same hon. gentleman.
Now, sir, I wish to begin with the Mac-Quarrie committee report. I remind the house that that committee was appointed to study the whole Combines Investigation Act and its operations. It was not the committee's idea that it should be called upon to divorce one particular segment of the problem from the whole, and make an interim report on that. This was the government's idea. I invite hon. members to consider the circumstances under which that report was made. Let us recall that the government has been under strong attack for a long time over its failure to grapple with the problems rising in the wake of the high cost of living and inflation. Having done nothing in that direction, as a matter of fact having heaped fuel on the fires of inflation by their outrageous taxation policies, the government was looking about for some means of distracting public attention. Apparently one member of the government came up with what he was sure was a bright idea.
That hon. minister had need of a bright idea, particularly on this subject. After parliament had been summoned a hurry-up

Combines Investigation Act call was put through to the MacQuarrie committee asking that committee to bring in an interim report on this one particular subject, detached from the remainder of the considerations of the Combines Investigation Act, and so with great speed that committee wrote this report. The haste in the writing of the report is reflected in almost every line of it. It is reflected most of all, I think, in the clear departure contemplated by this report from the essential principle of the Combines Investigation Act, to which I hope to return later in my remarks. We see this report going forward to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) who, as I have said, had some special reason for wanting to come up with a bright idea about the Combines Investigation Act because of the way in which he himself in 1949 had committed a flagrant and outrageous breach of that act, which breach continued for a year or more and made him the No. 1 lawbreaker in Canada. It was not thought such a bad idea, apparently, for him to come up with some proposal that would make it appear as though he were going to do something constructive under the Combines Investigation Act. The stage was carefully set on the eve of the opening of parliament.
When we look at this report from the MacQuarrie committee we see, in the first place, that it is open to two very strong criticisms. No one can read that report without concluding that it is merely a catalogue of opinions. There is no evidence in that report, and that is the first obvious weakness. Mr. McGregor said the committee had before it no statistical evidence. We do not know what they had before them or what they had not, because in this report they have not told us what evidence they had before them.
The second great weakness of this report is that it simply sidesteps the problem of loss leaders. The MacQuarrie committee recognized the formidable nature of this problem of loss leaders, and in the concluding paragraph of the report they say:
As to the "loss leader" device, the committee believes that it is a monopolistic practice which does not promote general welfare and therefore considers that it is not compatible with the public interest.
The MacQuarrie committee stopped there. They have brought forward no recommendations for coping with the formidable problem of the loss leader. They did not do so, sir, for the interesting reason which is to be found in the final sentence of the report:
. . . and the committee, therefore, does not think it imperative to make an immediate and hasty recommendation regarding that practice.
If the MacQuarrie committee would have regarded it as hasty to try to formulate some

recommendations for coping with the problem of loss leaders, then what is to be said of the way this report has been jammed through a parliamentary committee, and now the government is attempting to thrust it down our throats?
Apart from the lack of any policy to cope with this great problem of the loss leader, what weight is to be attached to this report? In cases of this kind one naturally looks with respect at the authors. One wishes to attribute to a report of this kind whatever measure of authority stands behind such individuals as compose the committee. As to the fact that one member of the committee was a judge, I think it is not unusual that the opinions of judges are subject to appeal; but when those opinions or judgments go before a court of appeal the conclusions are weighed in the light of the evidence. No member of this House of Commons can today form an intelligent judgment of the MacQuarrie committee's report because we do not know what evidence, if any, that committee had before it on which it based those conclusions.
As to the learned professors who composed the balance of the personnel of the committee, especially when hon. members like the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) invited the committee to sit down and accept without question anything that fell from the lips or pens of these eminent gentlemen, I think it is only fair to observe that anybody working under the pressure that apparently this committee was obliged to, under the direction from the government of September 10, could easily make mistakes. There is not, I think, any of these gentlemen who can claim to be infallible. I think it is only fair to observe that men working under pressure, whether of time or of an importunate and ambitious minister of the crown, can easily make mistakes.
How practical is the report? The authority of the report depends to some extent on the experience of the authors, and I think it is only fair to observe in passing that if this report has to stand on the strength of the opinion of the authorities and has no evidence to support it, then we can only observe in all fairness that none of these worthy gentlemen has had any experience in merchandising; and certainly one of them was out of the country all last summer and was quite busy when he got back to Kingston in September, and I greatly doubt if he had much time to devote to the writing of this report.
I said in the committee, and I say it in the House of Commons, that given the evidence on this important question of resale price maintenance the members of the House of

Commons, with their training, with the technique they have of applying their minds to political and economic questions, and with their experience, are just as capable of f orming an* intelligent conclusion on a question that has both economic and political aspects to it as are any members of any royal commission.
I therefore say to you, sir, that the House of Commons ought to have the evidence on this question. The House of Commons has not been given the evidence. There is not a member of this house who can claim, in making the decision which the government asks him to make, that he is making an informed decision in the light of evidence and facts. If he does so he is flying in the face of truth. The fact of the matter is-and it is crystal clear after what has happened in these recent days-that the government's minds were made up before this report was ever received. They were simply looking for an opportunity to buttress a recommendation that was being written into the throne speech. They might just as well have foregone the parliamentary committee because their minds were made up before that committee was ever appointed.
It is not unfair to comment, sir, that it was the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson), when he was meeting the people who were coming before him with complaints, problems and protests about what the government was doing, who cooed away in their ears and said to them; "You have nothing to fear from this. Coldwell is pushing us hard for price control and we must have something that we can hold out in front of the people. This is what we are going to do. It will not hurt you. You just be quiet, and this is what we will dangle out in front of the people." That is the sort of birth this ugly child has had.

Now, I wish to make it clear that we members of the official opposition went into that committee with an open mind on the subject. We asked that Mr. McGregor be called. You would think that Mr. McGregor had suddenly become a saint today. Perhaps the government should be reminded that it was because of the cloud this government

cast upon him that he tendered his resignation two years ago, because as a self-respecting citizen he would not submit any longer to the indignities cast upon him by this government. We of the official opposition wanted to have the evidence of Mr. McGregor, with his long experience. We make no apology for asking that he testify. Let those apologize rather who were responsible for refusing to hear other people who were entitled to appear before the parliamentary committee, and who thus prevented justice being done in the name of the Canadian people.
And, sir, the committee got under way. The prevailing idea at first was that we would preserve balance. The idea was that we would hear those in favour of resale price maintenance and also hear those against it. The hon. member for Kamloops and I sat in on the steering committee and it was decided that we would alternate the witnesses, first one opposed to price maintenance, then one favouring it, so that this committee would have a balanced presentation, and so that through the press the public would have a balanced report.
The first organization called was already on record as against resale price maintenance. I refer to the Canadian Congress of Labour. The alternating of witnesses in this manner was proceeded with for a few days, until there was a meeting of the steering committee after the first week or ten days. By that time it had become clear that we could not hope to conclude the work upon which we were embarked. The fact was clearly conceded by the representatives of the other parties present when the chairman, who was in a more responsible mood than today, said, "If we do not push this through to a conclusion at this session you fellows"-and he turned to my friend from Kamloops and myself- "will be criticizing us for not pushing it through." We said "No", that the committee could not be criticized if it did not fully accomplish what was an impossible task, at this session, although criticism could attach to the government for starting on something that had not been properly considered before it was begun, and it would have to take the responsibility and the criticism for that.
The chairman said he would talk with the minister about it, come back and make a report. That was at the end of one week. It must have been a hectic weekend in the Liberal party, because when the committee assembled at the first of the next week all was changed. We were told that this committee was going to report at this session. We were told that from that point on there would be no time to hear both sides of the question. We were told there would be no
Combines Investigation Act opportunity to appear afforded to those who had put in briefs in opposition to resale price maintenance. We were told that a deadline would be fixed for the conclusion of the hearing, and that it did not matter from that point on how much we protested-we, of the official opposition, those of us who wanted to hear both sides of the question and get all the facts-we were told it did not matter. Taking his instructions from the government, through the Minister of Justice, the chairman of the committee applied the guillotine. From that time on the chairman of the committee functioned as a guillotinist; and he did it under the direction of the Minister of Justice.
If that is justice, then we think we had better recast in this House of Commons, very soon, our idea of justice.

Their time, as well as the time of the individual members of the committee, was rationed. In the third place, there were many who applied to be heard and who were refused permission. Many of them represented retail interests and associations in this country. They represented retail merchants, numbering thousands of people in the ranks. Then, in addition, there

were those who did not appear before the committee and who did not apply for hearing because they realized the futility of it, in the light of the ruling which had been made.

Eaton Company had made their position public at an early date, a position which must have given great comfort to the government. Why were not they called?
