But the committee sided with the government to apply the guillotine in order to prevent the committee from having the evidence of T. Eaton Company Limited, the largest departmental store in Canada. Our attempts in the opposition to make that committee really effective for the purpose of obtaining information were thwarted by the majority on the committee.

I can assure you that I did not impute dishonesty to any member of the house. I did impute a great deal of deliberate obstruction in the committee by the government majority on the committee.
Therefore, for these reasons I for one cannot accept the report of the MacQuarrie committee without evidence which would enable me to test the validity of its conclusions. I am not prepared to do anything to condone the gagging of this parliamentary committee and the suppression by the majority on that committee of necessary evidence. I recognize

that this question of resale price maintenance is a very large and important question and therefore it should have careful and ample consideration. The course that has been followed here by the government in gagging the committee is calculated to prevent any fair assessment of the arguments that have been submitted.
When we are asked by hon. members, as we were by the hon. member for Coast-Capilano in his flight of oratory this afternoon, to picture resale price maintenance as being a vicious system today, I invite him to remember, because evidently his memory needs some jogging, that this practice has grown up and reached its present extent largely during the lifetime of the present government. It did so while a man was Prime Minister in this country who claimed to be the father of the Combines Investigation Act and who looked with no little favour and respect upon Mr. McGregor. I just ask hon. members of the house, before they get too far over the brink on this question, before they go too far in their denunciation of resale price maintenance, to recall that the practice grew up under the government of the late Mr. Mackenzie King, who manifested a great interest in combines. If the practice is as vicious as the hon. member for Coast-Capilano pictured it to be this afternoon, I wonder what has been going on in this house since 1935. Did we have to wait until the arrival of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) in the house to come up with the discovery of this problem in all its iniquity, as it was described to us today? Is he the only man who has recognized the problem at all? Is he the only man who has been able to diagnose it and see it in its true dark light? Is he the only man who is capable of conceiving a solution? Is he the only man that has been at all on his job? If so, why was not something done from 1935 to 1949, if the facts were as they have been put before us this afternoon; and I for one say that they are not.
In view of the way hon. members opposite have helped to exhaust my time by their interruptions I am simply going to make a few assertions as to the effect of the limited evidence that was received.
First, the practice of resale price maintenance has grown up as a defence of small retailers against the pressure of big interests. It is not a practice dictated or defended by so-called big interests. Mr. McGregor made it quite clear that the practice is wanted by the retailers, rather than the manufacturers. The Minister of Justice talks about the expensive establishment, on the one hand,
Combines Investigation Act and the plain cash and carry store, on the other. He got a little bit confused. Apparently the plain cash and carry stores are the chain stores, and undoubtedly they will take great comfort from what the Minister of Justice said yesterday.
Second, the principal danger against which resale price maintenance protects the small retailer is the practice of loss leaders. It is the branded, price-maintained articles that are found most suitable for exploitation as loss leaders.
Third, the loss leader is a thoroughly vicious practice. That has been made perfectly clear by a great number of authorities.
Fourth, there is no adequate alternative protection against the loss leader. That was made abundantly clear by Mr. McGregor in his evidence. It is made abundantly clear by the way the MacQuarrie committee spoke of it. It was made abundantly clear by the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) when he submitted draft legislation on the subject which the committee did not accept as workable. Section 498A of the Criminal Code does not meet this problem of the loss leader, as Mr. Ralston and Mr. Ilsley said in their speeches on June 10, 1935.
Fifth, resale price maintenance has brought stability into the retail trades affected. In the house we have heard a great deal of talk about the necessity of orderly marketing for farmers. It would not be amiss to point out the value of orderly marketing in the retail trades.
Sixth, there is no proof that the consuming public has been hurt by resale price maintenance. On the contrary, the evidence shows that this practice has provided a guarantee of quality and has increased the number of outlets. In that way it has encouraged increased competition. Then the margin of profit is lower on branded than on nonbranded articles. Moreover the margin of profit on branded articles has risen less than on the non-branded in the sellers' market of recent years. The manufacturer sets the margin with a view to making the purchase of his product attractive to the public.
Seventh, there is no proof that the consuming public will benefit from a ban on resale price maintenance. Under that point I cite these four circumstances:
(a)	If loss leadering reduces prices of branded articles, the retailers tell us they would have to make up that loss by raising the prices on non-branded articles or go out of business, and in that way reduce competition.

Combines Investigation Act
(b)	Elimination of retail outlets means less competition and less service to the public.
(c)	Concentration of economic power in the
hands of chains and big, powerful retail outlets will not benefit the consumer. Any immediate advantage will be of little benefit in view of the long-term disadvantage that he will suffer from growing monopoly in retail outlets.	*
(d)	The manufacturer may be driven, we were told, to protect himself against the chains and big retailers by himself going into the retail business. This will not make for efficiency. In this connection I wish to deal with the reference by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) last night to Henry Ford and his system. Let me tell the Minister of Justice that Henry Ford is not an example of any ban on resale price maintenance. Henry Ford went into the retail business as well as the manufacturing business. The example was far-fetched. Then I come to my next point.
Eighth, there is no proof that the elimination of resale price maintenance will reduce the cost of living. The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) said so when he spoke on this subject on October 15. He said it would make no material reduction in the cost of living. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) said the same thing today. We know of course that the Minister of Justice said something different yesterday, and the hon. member for Coast-Capilano said the opposite this afternoon. I would just as soon take the view of the Prime Minister and the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar as I would the view of the Minister of Justice and the voluble member for Coast-Capilano. Before anybody becomes too hopeful of price reductions he would do well to read an editorial in the Canadian Unionist, the journal of the Canadian Congress of Labour, of December, 1951 in which I read the following:
The enquiry-
That is the one into resale price maintenance.
-is continuing, and has stirred up considerable interest throughout Canada, but there is no reason to believe that, even if the legislation is passed, it will bring about any reduction in the cost of living.
That is only sound common sense and fact.

Mr. Speaker, as I was privileged to be a member of the joint parliamentary committee on combines legislation I feel I should make some attempt to explain to my constituents as best I can the reasons why I support this legislation. The great task and the great challenge that confronts this generation is to make democracy work. Democracy cannot work unless the people understand and play their full part. The word "people" includes every one of us. It includes producers, consumers, manufacturers, wholesalers, retailers, members of the learned professions and members of parliament. In a democracy such as ours the part of the people is just as important, perhaps even more so, than the part of government. It is obvious that the people cannot play their part and democracy cannot work unless we have an enlightened public opinion.
The enemies of democracy recognize this and spare no effort to confuse public opinion whenever the opportunity offers. The fact that some confusion of public opinion exists is shown by the tendency to make conflicting demands, demands which are contradictory to the point of being mutually exclusive. For example, we have the cry go up for a curb on inflation, and at the same time a demand for greater public expenditure. We get a demand for less taxation on the one hand and at the

same time a cry for increased social benefit payments on the other. We get a demand for greater individual freedom and at the same time a demand for more government control. In the parliamentary committee on combines legislation we had a demand for more freedom of individual enterprise and at the same time a demand for less competition. It is obvious that we cannot have one without the other. Competition is the price that we must be prepared to pay for freedom of enterprise.
Parliament is a deliberative body, and we refer to it with pride as the highest court in the land. We should be very careful not to reduce parliament to the level of a sounding board. This is one place to which the people should be able to look with confidence that they will find the truth, and it is our job to see that they get the truth and the whole truth. To do that we must separate facts from opinions, suppositions and speculations, and see that we place the proper labels on each so the people will be able to give to each one its proper value and thus be able to perform their democratic function.
The present combines legislation makes it illegal for any person or corporation to make an agreement with another person or corporation for the purpose of controlling prices and eliminating competition. It does not, however, in its present form prevent any person or corporation from controlling prices and eliminating competition by means of a series of vertical agreements between the manufacturer and the distributor. The system whereby a dealer agrees to sell an article at a price fixed by the manufacturer is known as resale price maintenance. Some manufacturers have used this device to control prices and evade present legislation. The only solution to this problem is to strengthen the present law by the abolition of price maintenance.
Unfortunately we cannot discuss price maintenance without getting involved in some discussion of prices in general, price levels, profit margins, mark-ups, the cost of living, inflation and other related topics which are of intense public interest. But we should never lose sight of the fact that interesting though these topics are they are nevertheless only secondary considerations. The real purpose of this legislation is to prevent a person or corporation from evading the present law. The real purpose of this legislation is not to combat inflation, not to reduce the cost of living, but to prevent corporations from controlling prices and eliminating competition. And the primary question before this house is simply, shall we retain resale price maintenance and allow corporations to continue
Combines Investigation Act evading the law, or shall we abolish price maintenance and prevent them from doing so?
The position of the government on this matter is indicated by the stand they have taken on government price control in general. In the words of one of the witnesses, this government has resolutely set its face against the imposition of over-all government price control. It would be very inconsistent for the government to take that stand with regard to government control of prices and at the same time sanction a system of private control. Furthermore, the government made a commitment to the people of this nation to abolish price maintenance. When that commitment became known a great deal of organized opposition developed. The government decided to set up a committee so the opponents of this legislation would be afforded an opportunity to state their case in public and to make useful suggestions. I for one am grateful to the government for setting up this committee. Personally I think it was a very wise move; otherwise thousands of simple people like myself would never have had an opportunity of understanding the nature of this problem.
When the committee was set up, the government were charged with retreating from their position, of stalling and of foregoing their commitments. I must confess, Mr. Speaker, that I was very much surprised to find that the same people who accused the government of stalling, turned around in committee and accused them of steamrolling, of railroading the legislation, of making snap decisions without sufficient evidence and without sufficient study.
Although the committee was specifically charged with a study of the recommendations contained in the MacQuarrie report, it should be borne in mind that this was not the only evidence available to the government and to the committee on this subject. A wealth of information was available from many sources. To mention a few there was the royal commission on prices known as the Curtis report; the Lloyd Jacob report of Britain; the British white paper; the debate in the British House of Commons last June; the studies and reports of various United States federal and state organizations; the royal commission on the cost of living in Newfoundland, 1950, and the information and evidence arising from investigations and prosecutions of the federal combines commission.
In general all of this evidence, while admitting that price maintenance does afford some advantages, tends to the general conclusion that the disadvantages greatly outweigh the



Combines Investigation Act advantages, and that price maintenance should be abolished in the public interest.
In addition to all this evidence there were the large number of briefs which were presented to the committee, and which in many cases were supplemented by verbal evidence from witnesses who appeared before the committee. These witnesses were sharply divided into two main groups. The masses of the people as represented generally by the great labour organizations, the large consumer organizations and the co-operative unions, submitted briefs requesting that price maintenance be abolished. With the exception of a few large retail firms, manufacturers' organizations and associations of retailers and wholesalers submitted briefs requesting that price maintenance be retained.
The merits and demerits of price maintenance in itself and its effect on the cost of living are, as I have already said, secondary considerations and important only in so far as they relate to the primary question as to whether any person or corporation should be permitted to use this device to control prices and eliminate competition. However, since so much discussion has revolved around the topic of price maintenance in itself, perhaps it would be worth-while to list a few of the main arguments presented for and against this practice. Those opposed to the practice of price maintenance claim that it should be abolished because (1) it is a system	of private	law	privately	enforcedwithout reference to any court of law; (2) it eliminates competition in distribution; (3) it fosters	competition	between manufacturersfor the goodwill of retailers so that manufacturers outbid each other, offering higher margins, higher mark-ups and greater profits to the retailer and hence higher and higher prices;	(4) it prevents	the more	efficientretailer from passing on the benefits of his efficiency to the consumer in the form of lower prices; (5) it multiplies retail outlets far beyond what is necessary and (6) resale price maintenance	has	increased	greatly
during the past 20 years and is still increasing at an alarming rate.
Those who wish to retain resale price maintenance claim that it should be retained because (1) it protects the small dealer from the predatory price cutting practices of larger and financially stronger firms; (2) it equalizes prices from one end of the country to the other; (3) it keeps prices lower because nationally advertised products are easier to sell and therefore require lower mark-ups; (4) it protects the rights of manufacturers who had built up a national demand for their products; (5) it protects the prestige enjoyed by branded products; (6) it stabilizes production and therefore the nation's economy; and
fMr. Carter.]
(7) if resale price maintenance were abolished many smaller dealers would be forced out of business.
The bulk of the evidence given in support of the retention of resale price maintenance consisted mainly of opinions, suppositions and fears largely based on lack of faith in their fellow man. What few facts did emerge tended to refute their claims.
We are all sympathetic to the little man, whether he is a manufacturer, jobber or retailer. The evidence presented to the committee showed that the efficiency of a business did not increase with its size. Though larger firms secured larger discounts by means of mass buying, yet that advantage was largely offset by the lower overhead and lower operating costs of the little man; and as the hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Sinclair) has pointed out, also because the little man was largely exempt from corporation taxes. As a result small firms have been able to stay in business and compete with chain stores, large department stores and corporations. The prediction of casualties amongst dealers is not borne out by the evidence, nor by the experience in the grocery trade where competition is fierce and where less than 1 per cent of the goods sold is protected by price maintenance. It is possible that a number of firms will go out of business, because in many cases the number of retail outlets is far greater than the total turnover warrants. The tendency of resale price maintenance is to raise prices to a level where all can stay in business, regardless of the volume of the turnover and regardless of the efficiency of the individual firm.
A great deal of thought was also given to the practice of price cutting known as the loss leader. There is reason to believe that once the background of fixed prices has been removed, the loss leader will lose a great deal of its effectiveness. It was found that this practice assumed so many forms it was practically impossible of definition, and the general conclusion reached was that section 498A of the Criminal Code afforded as much protection as any legislation that can be devised until the problem has assumed more definite and concrete proportions.
The evidence also showed that, other factors being equal or comparable-factors such as geography, wealth, purchasing power, and so on-prices tended to be lower in those areas where price maintenance had been abolished. Last evening the minister pointed out the experience in the United States, where comparisons were possible between four states with price maintenance and four comparable states where price maintenance had been abolished.

In Canada the only comparison possible is in the province of Newfoundland. We Newfoundlanders can speak from personal experience, because we had the doubtful benefit of price maintenance thrust upon us almost overnight. Before confederation price maintenance was not practised in Newfoundland, and its full and sudden impact became apparent almost immediately after confederation. The hon. member for Coast-Capilano has referred to the example of the No. 6 dry cell ignition battery which is an important item for our fishermen. The reference to this item is contained in chapter 10 of the report of the royal commission on the cost of living in Newfoundland, 1950, and was brought to the attention of the committee in a brief submitted by the Newfoundland co-operative union.

The royal commission points out on page 78 of its report:
In several hardware lines in which there is resale price maintenance, the setting of prices has thus required dealers to take mark-ups definitely higher than those that had prevailed under more open competition. The dealers, doubtless, often had no serious objection to doing so.
On page 79 of the commission report, 1 find this:
Resale price maintenance since confederation has had a marked effect. It has brought many prices in line with national prices. At the same time, it has tended to place prices of drugs, some women's and other clothing, and many hardware and electrical goods above the levels they might have reached if no resale prices had been suggested after confederation.
The witnesses who appeared before the committee laid a great deal of stress on the prestige enjoyed by branded products, which they maintained should be protected. The extent to which the consumer is forced to pay for the prestige of branded products is abundantly illustrated by the evidence concerning aspirin tablets, to which the hon. member for Coast-Capilano referred earlier. Bayer's aspirin tablets retail at 79 cents for 100, while unbranded tablets of the same chemical formula and conforming in every way with the requirements of the Food and Drugs Act retail at only 19 cents per 100 tablets. Naturally, it pays the druggist well to push the sale of Bayer's aspirin in preference to the unbranded tablet.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I should like to make one brief reference to a matter which concerned me, not only as a member of the committee but as a new Canadian. It relates to the number of witnesses representing manufacturers, wholesalers and retailers, who expressed fear, suspicion and mistrust in their fellow members in the organizations which they represented. If their fears were genuine, we are asked to believe that our leading businessmen, the managers of our most prominent firms, are extremely greedy and selfish individuals who are just waiting for an opportunity to resort to the law of the jungle, and who will stop at nothing to eliminate their weaker and less fortunate competitors. That there

Combines Investigation Act is some greed and selfishness we must admit. Otherwise there would be no need for any combines legislation at all. But I find it extremely difficult to believe that the majority of our businessmen are very different from the rest of us in that respect. It is obvious that we cannot make people honest, nor can we remove greed and selfishness, simply by passing a law. It is a moral problem rather than a legal or economic problem, and while legislation is necessary, a more positive approach is required.
The evidence that a more positive approach is possible and that a positive answer to this problem exists is contained in a book which I have lately read and which is entitled "World Rebuilt" by Peter Howard. This book is a record of events that are taking place at the present time and which are destined to change the course of history. I was impressed with the wealth of evidence that industry, business and management all over the free world are awakening to a new sense of morality and of responsibility for the nation and for the democratic way of life. "The old order changeth, yielding place to new." Whether we are prepared' to admit it or not, a new order is coming into existence. A new world is being built, and the slogan "business as usual" has long been out of date.
Stalin, in a lecture to his communist leaders at Moscow, is reported to have said: If capitalism could adapt its production not to the getting of maximum profits but to the systematic improvement of the masses of the people, then there would be no crisis; but then capitalism would not be capitalism.
The stories of such eminent and internationally famous businessmen as Dr. Heinrich Kost, managing director of the Rhein-prensen Company and chairman of the German coal board; of Robert Tilge, French industrialist and secretary of the employers federation of northern France; of Charles Redele, large producer of foodstuffs in Holland; and many others as related by Peter Howard, all testify to the fact that capitalism is being gripped by a much greater idea than the mere accumulation of profits and that in industry, business, management and labour a new type of businessman is emerging to match the new era.
I strongly recommend this book to every member of parliament, to every businessman and to every labour leader in Canada if only for the purpose of reading the thrilling story of the National Airlines in the United States. This company was on the point of being dismembered and broken up because of bad relations between management and

pilots. At that point the president, George Baker, began to apply this new thinking and this new positive approach to the problem, with the amazing result that within the space of a few months his balance sheet changed from a deficit to a profit of half a million dollars per month. I think that amply illustrates the soundness of this positive approach to business and management problems.
In a statement made in Washington, D.C., on May 1, 1951, Mr. D. W. Rentzel. chairman of the civil aeronautics board, said:
To those familiar with the long history of bitter and acrimonious dispute, the transformation in the attitude of the parties from one of suspicion and hostility to an attitude of mutual co-operation and trust has been little short of miraculous.
That statement which I have quoted referred to the National Airlines.
We Canadians are richly blessed in that we have inherited the most favoured nation *on the face of the earth. To a large extent the fate of this nation and of this people rests in the hands of our businessmen. Underproduction, through the selfish application of the economics of scarcity, can easily push our economy over the border from inflation to disastrous deflation.
Price determination is not a matter of government control nor of private law. It is simply a matter of manufacturer, wholesaler and retailer each honestly facing the facts and making a moral decision based on what is right having due regard for the interests of the consumer and the welfare of the nation, as well as for his own individual interest.
During world war II Canadian business astonished the world with its amazing achievements. I feel confident, Mr. Speaker, that when they realize the full extent of their national responsibilities Canadian businessmen will again prove equal to this even greater challenge which is the mark of our time.

Mr. Speaker, after that last remark I think 1 should start out by saying that now I have heard everything. The hon. member for Burin-Burgeo (Mr. Carter) who has just taken his seat stated that all consumers were in favour of this legislation, and by listing the various people who were against it he made the implication that all business was against this legislation. I think I should not go on with the remarks I propose to make without drawing attention to this statement because it is so utterly opposed to what is actually the case. We sat in this committee for some time, and we heard businessmen both for and against. We had from businessmen briefs both for and against the legislation. We had briefs-most of them from the consumer angle, I grant you-either for or partly for the legislation. I would not say they were entirely in favour of the legislation.
I should like to start, Mr. Speaker, by trying to bring this question out of the realm of academic debate and down to a practical position, and to ask bluntly these questions: Who will benefit by this legislation? Who will suffer from it? Why is it being introduced? I do not think for a moment that anyone is under any misapprehension as to who will benefit. Certainly those merchandisers who are manufacturers of private brands, who are in the fortunate position of being at one and the same time the manufacturer and their own retailer, stand to benefit from this legislation.
Who will suffer? Well, the small businessman will suffer, and the consumer will suffer. I have been interested to hear the debate which	has	taken	place thus farbecause at some place in almost every speech someone has	said,	"We	love the smallbusinessman, but-".	I do not think the
small businessman is under any misapprehension about the legislation at all. I do think that a great many consumers are misled.
I intend to deal with that at a later point, but I should	like to go	on now and askthis question:	Why	is this	legislation being
introduced? Is it being introduced to bring down the cost of living? I do not believe it is, because all the government members have been very careful to say that it will have no effect on the cost of living. The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) himself early in the session said he did not expect that the introduction of this legislation would have any effect whatever on the cost of living.
I personally went to some pains to do a piece of research on this point. I took the cost of living index items and broke them down into those which were price controlled and those which were not price controlled.
Combines Investigation Act And I might say that a large part of those which are under a resale price maintenance policy are under a policy dictated by a government, either federal or provincial. Some of the other items are under other forms of price maintenance, such as transportation and communications. When you break it all down, it comes out to something like this: The food items make up 31 per cent of the cost of living index. Of that total, 1/15 of 1 per cent are under a rigid price maintenance policy. Then rentals make up 19 per cent; fuel and light, 6 per cent; clothing, 12 per cent; home furnishings, 9 per cent and miscellaneous, 23 per cent. When you take the various weights- I hope I have done it correctly-and take the number of items which are maintained and take the percentage that is of the total weight, it finally comes down to 6-3 per cent of the total.
As I said before, some of the items which are maintained will not be changed anyway. You will not change railway fares; you will not change doctors' fees; you will not change telephone bills; you will not change many other things. You will not change transportation costs, because these are things that cannot be changed by this legislation. Therefore if we took a wildly optimistic view of what this might do to the cost of living, and said that on the over-all basis the whole cost of living might drop on these items by 5 per cent, then we would have -31 per cent of the cost of living.
I think I have been well repaid for the work I did on this, because it has shown me how foolish is any argument which would try to support the belief that this will have any effect at all on the cost of living. Yet I believe many consumers in this country are under the impression, rightly or wrongly, that this legislation is being brought down to remedy in some way the situation in which we find ourselves today because of the greatly increased cost of living. So perhaps the answer to the question as to why this legislation is being introduced is this: while it might not bring down the cost of living, it may very well be that it has been brought in as an answer to the pressure from an inflation-weary country. Undoubtedly this pressure has prompted the government to do something. Far from adopting a course which might have had some effect on combines legislation, this government has chosen to hide behind a smokescreen of resale price maintenance, to attempt by eliminating this practice to demonstrate to the people of Canada that it has taken action, at the same time pleasing those who have monopolistic tendencies by removing one of the impediments to the pursuit of certain trade practices.

Combines Investigation Act
This legislation is not going to help the consumer. It is not going to do a thing for the pensioners who are living on the same pensions but with a greatly increased cost of living. It is not going to help the elderly people one bit. It is not going to be of any service at all to the homemaker. The opening paragraph of the brief presented to the committee by the Canadian Congress of Labour, as it is set out at page 73 of the proceedings of the committee, states:
The congress does not believe that either the Combines Investigation Act (with the related provisions of the Criminal Code) or the prohibition of resale price maintenance, will have any marked effect on the cost of living.
The minister in his remarks last night made reference to suggested prices. I take it I am correct in believing that he meant he had no personal axe to grind against those who were suggesting resale prices. I think there is a great deal of doubt in the minds of committee members and others as to what constitutes a maintained price and what constitutes a suggested price. We talked about this to some extent in the committee. Mr. McGregor had some things to say in this connection at page 614 of the evidence. I questioned him as follows:
To what extent would you think control of suggested resale prices might go? To the extent of placing a price on a product? A. It might be, yes.
Q. Would you think it would not be illegal under the proposed legislation to put a price on a label or a bottle or a shirt? A. No, under this particular proposal it does not seem that it would. This bill does not go the whole hog but it may be that it would prevent the enforced price. There is still a lot going on in suggested prices where really competition is not working and you might later, in a few years hence, find it is doing damage and have to deal with it.
Q. You say that the next step may be the abolition of the suggested price? A. It may be that a situation will develop where competition is not working. Perhaps not, and if not I think it should be left free. As long as a man is free and does not have to adopt the suggestion of the manufacturer-
You will notice the witness says that a man does not have to adopt the suggestion of the manufacturer. That is a rather foolish statement because if it is not enforced, then he certainly does not have to adopt it. The answer continues:	.
As long as a man is free and does not have to adopt the suggestion of the manufacturer, then I think probably it is better to have the form of the bill as it is here.
I submit here, as I did in the committee, that the number of strictly maintained lines is negligible. Most are suggested and preserved as such as long as business is continuing on an even tenor. This brings up two possibilities. The first is that this legislation will open the door for the destruction of business by encouraging an all-out attack on famous brands, those items which are

maintained. We have seen what happens when a price war is started in connection with one or two articles. The whole business of the community is disrupted, on both maintained and non-maintained lines. If that does not happen, then there is the possibility that an even more sinister intent is present in the enforcement of this legislation and such regulations as may be made thereunder than appears at the moment.
I should like to refer for a few minutes to the evidence presented in the committee. First, I should like to call your attention to a phrase which occurs in the speech from the throne, "without impairing our free institutions". I think we all agree that freedom is something not easily defined. We have always claimed that one of the greatest products of freedom is our courts of justice. There is a saying abroad, I do not know how true it is in actual practice, that a man is innocent until he is proved guilty. This inquiry was in reverse. A charge was levelled against these people who operated, either at the manufacturing or retailing level, under a system of resale price maintenance. In effect the government said, "You are guilty; you prove that you are innocent". Far from the government proving that they were guilty, far from the government proving that the results of price maintenance worked to the disadvantage of the consumer, they simply made a bald statement.
I would remind hon. members that in the examination that followed the presentation of the brief by the Canadian Congress of Labour the witness stated that if they could be convinced that resale price maintenance worked to the advantage rather than the disadvantage of the consumer, they would support it. They were not convinced that it worked to the disadvantage of the consumer.
In the brief presented by the Trades and Labour Congress they said they were not quite satisfied that a case had been made out against resale price maintenance. In spite of that, statements are made repeatedly in this house that all consumers are against resale price maintenance. The fact is that the two largest groups representing consumers have both said they have had no proof that resale price maintenance is not to the advantage of the consumer.
Statement after statement was made and then the accused, if we can use that term for the businessman of Canada, was told to defend himself. When he proceeded to do so he was told that he had given no proof, that he had presented no figures. He then said he would bring figures. I refer hon. members to pages 48'9, 490 and 491 of the proceedings of the committee. While they

do not set out the results of an exhaustive study, hon. members will find there a sample of the type of thing that could be and was produced. The gentleman who produced those figures stated quite bluntly that some were in favour of his argument and some were opposed to it. He took them as they came on a selected list of articles and presented what he had. That was the kind of evidence we should have had in a more exhaustive form from other people engaged in business. At times the committee proceedings took on the complexion of a criminal trial instead of an inquiry. I deplored the manner in which expert witnesses were abused and I might say almost insulted at times.
For a few minutes I should like to talk about the small businessman. I think of him first as being a distributor of needed goods. Within the last six or seven years we faced a situation in this country where many of the articles sorely needed by the consumer were in very short supply. Some articles were rationed, while others were distributed under a sort of voluntary rationing system. In some cases the manufacturer and the first distributor were called upon by the regulations of the wartime prices and trade board to distribute the product which was in short supply on a pro rata basis to their customers on the basis of the historical pattern of supply which showed on their books. It frequently happened that even at the wholesale level some fairly good-sized merchants got only half a case of certain tinned goods. That was particularly true of salmon, which was in very short supply. A case would go out to the retailer, who knew that he had to distribute it to all his customers. He had to use his own judgment as to who was going to get the goods. So he distributed his goods according to a similar historical pattern of trade. He knew thet certain customers habitually bought certain articles, so he saved some for them. The same was true of other lines, such as soaps.
I am sure that there is not a housewife in this country who does not remember when she did one of two things. Either she stood in line for a long time in a store where she had heard there was a supply of goods and where the goods were distributed on an impersonal basis of first come first served. Maybe she got some and maybe she did not. Or if she had been in the habit of dealing with one store she knew she could depend on that storekeeper to see that she got her fair share.
Some peculiar statements have been made during the course of this debate. I look back on this pattern of distribution with which I was very familiar, and I find it very difficult to make it fit in with some of the statements that have been made. From my knowledge

of the small businessman I find it difficult to understand how the minister could say that after all the small businessman does not pay any corporation tax. I know he does not pay any corporation tax. He pays his personal income tax at the personal rate on the total amount of money his business makes, whether he withdraws it or whether he does not, and he pays even on the profit he makes which he leaves in his business for expansion or for the purchase of new equipment. He does not benefit by the system which is in effect for corporations whereby he is permitted to withdraw his salary and then pay at the lower rate of corporation tax for small incorporated businesses. I am sure the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) will bear me out in that. I believe the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) was a little mistaken when he made that remark, and I am sure if he would investigate it he would wish to withdraw it.
Several things have not yet been touched in the course of this debate. I should like to build up for the house a picture of the type of thing that is likely to happen if the government persists in passing this legislation. We will undoubtedly have a raid on name brands. We will have a race for the lowest price. In the race for the lowest price, which will probably see keen competition between large outlets that can well afford it, the poor little fellow on the same street is going to see the crowds just running past his door, not in but past. The next step will be a demand on the manufacturer to supply a product to meet a price. By that I mean this. We will suppose that a dealer has a brand name shirt which he sells for $5. When this competition develops his competitor will start to sell it for $4.75. Then he will sell it for $4.50, and finally a demand will be made on the manufacturer for a shirt which will retail for $3.99.
Who is going to say whether two inches less material has been put into that shirt, whether a lower grade of button has been used and whether-which may be a very serious thing when you consider the wearing qualities of a garment-a lower grade of thread has been used. During the war there were many instances where garments literally fell apart because of the low grade of thread which was available. These low grades may be used from choice if we are going to get into an all-out price-cutting war. Therefore we are faced with deterioration of quality, and it is serious matter. The extra coat of enamel on the saucepan disappears, the extra inch of material in the garment disappears, the extra ounce of vegetables in the soup disappears, all to meet a demand for an article at a price which will be competitive with that of the price cutter.

There are a great many people in this country who are entirely dependent upon the small retailer for many things, for service, credit, advice and even for a personal interest in their families. They depend upon him to keep them in food when they are out of work for a while, and that is a serious thing today when this country is witnessing the largest unemployment it has known for many years. The little fellow supports these people, and sometimes he never collects from them. He is the backbone of our economy; yet he was accused before the committee. Even his representative, the one organization which is closest to the small independent retailer, was refused a hearing before the committee. I know perfectly well the committee took the stand that the parent body, which represents all retailers in the Dominion of Canada, had had a hearing; but the policy adopted by the committee was broken when they agreed to hear other members of that parent body. Nevertheless they refused to hear the retail merchants association of Canada which represents several thousands of small independent retailers right across the country.

It reminds me of the situation which existed in the dark days. When a woman was accused of being a witch they took her out and threw her in the pond. If she swam she was a witch and they took her out and burned her. After I received a few telegrams from various business people in my riding I spent some time making inquiries to find out whether any of the small shopkeepers who operate their own individual businesses on the corners of my towns and cities had made any representations to have price maintenance brought into effect. I could not find an instance where one of the small shopkeepers had suggested that they wanted or had instigated price maintenance. Thus I must assume that although at the present time they are under the operation of price maintenance, it was not instigated at their request; and since it was not instigated at their request then I started to figure out who wants this thing. After listening to the very explicit and enlightening address by the member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming), I decided that the chain stores could buy a little cheaper in larger volume. If they could buy cheaper in larger volume and sell at maintained prices, they must make a much larger profit. After ascertaining that, I came to the conclusion that this price maintenance^ was something that was desired by big business.
For the moment I shall be honest and fair, and say that the small shopkeeper enjoys some benefits from this system; but what will happen to him eventually we are not prepared to say. Having had this brought to my attention, I did some research on it. I should like to give the house three situations showing various effects of taxes which, in some respects, answer the point raised by the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mrs. Fairclough). This situation is the result of the necessity for this country to defend itself. We on this side of the house do not like it, but this taxation is something which we have to endure. I should like to explain to the house just what the effects of taxation are on the small businessman and the large businessman who is incorporated. I do not say these arguments will convince the opposition, because they are not easy to convince when they do not want to be convinced. But perhaps my arguments will explain why the Minister of Justice asked the MacQuarrie

committee to present a special report, and why this legislation was introduced at this session.
Shortly after the last budget it became apparent that there was a change in the operation of the retail trade. Price fixation became rampant. It was necessary that something be done to correct this. The figures I shall present will prove beyond any doubt that this is the case. As an example, I have taken the case of a shopkeeper, married and with two children, who had a net profit- including interest from his investment and the results of his labour-of $10,000. This gentleman who owns his own business will pay income taxes amounting to $1,950. He has a net return for his labour of $8,050. Let us assume that a stockholder in an incorporated chain store had no other source of income, but operated a chain store next door to this private shopkeeper. What would he have to get in net profit, after wages and everything else had been paid, in order to receive as a dividend the same amount of money the small shopkeeper received? We find that for him to receive the same amount of net income -the individual who operates his own store is not incorporated-he would have to receive $20,100 in profits. For the operation of this country and for the defence of this country, this chain store stockholder would pay $12,050 in income taxes as against the $1,950 that the small shopkeeper would pay. But that is not the usual situation in these chain stores.
The person who has money invested in these incorporated chain stores generally is not the type of man who just invests his money and sits idly by living on the interest. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the past day and a half I have sensed a feeling of unreality in this chamber, due to the fact that I have heard Liberal speaker after Liberal speaker rise in his place and, in enunciating the principles of the Liberal party, say that anything to do with combines has always been very much looked down upon by the Liberal party and the Liberal government, and that such things have been ruthlessly prosecuted and stamped out.
Hearing this sort of thing time and again, I have had to pinch myself to make sure I was awake. Could this be the same Liberal party I was hearing about today that, only two short years ago, concealed for as long as ten months a report concerning an inquiry into an industry? That report came to light only because Mr. McGregor, who was then combines commissioner and about whom the government has so proudly boasted yesterday and today, became so revolted by the dishonesty of the course the government was pursuing in this connection that he resigned, and the whole thing then came to light.
I had to look over to the other side of the chamber to reassure myself that this was the same Liberal party, the same Liberal government these speakers were talking about, a government as they have said that has always been against combines, has stamped them out and done everything it could to make sure they did not exist. I looked over there and saw the same Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson), under whose department all this had happened, in protest against whose action the combines commissioner of that day had resigned. I looked a little further to his right and I saw the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), the man who had pulled
[Mr. Hosking.l
the strings that caused the Minister of Justice to take that very regrettable action. And then, Mr. Speaker, I asked myself this question: Just how white can a party paint itself, when such a very short time ago it was so very, very black?
I should like to go on now to say a few things about the proceedings of the committee on which I was privileged to serve during the last month. I speak of course of the committee which dealt with the question of resale ' price maintenance. After sitting for only a very few days on the committee, three things became obvious. First of all it became obvious that the government did not intend to pay even the slightest attention to the views of the small retailers who came forward to present their case. Second, it became clear that the loss leader was a very real threat to the business life of the small shopkeeper. Third, it was clear that the fair trade laws of the United States have proved to be more satisfactory to the people of that country than the abolition of price maintenance.
I should like to deal with those three matters, and I turn first to the consideration given to the point of view of the retailers. From the very first it was obvious that the small retailer was condemned before he even began to defend himself. The lawyers who were hired by the government, and who were supposed to be present as impartial questioners, had obviously been instructed by the government to destroy the case of the small retailer at the very first opportunity.
Their approach to the witnesses was that of a prosecuting attorney who was bent on proving that by trying to obtain a fair and stable price for his goods, the small shopkeeper is in some way guilty of a crime. It was in this atmosphere that the hearings of the committee were conducted, with the result that instead of the committee making a serious study of the facts in the case, the hearings were, in fact, a complete farce.
Secondly I should like to deal with the loss leader. Literally every witness who appeared before the committee stated that the loss leader is a very real threat to the life of the small shopkeeper. Among those who stated this view was no less a person than Mr. Fred McGregor, the former combines commissioner who, although he opposed resale price maintenance in theory, said that it was highly desirable to try to define the loss leader and to work out practical legislation to outlaw its operation.
Despite the overwhelming evidence that practical and enforceable legislation against the loss leader is needed, if price maintenance is to be abolished, the government steadfastly

refused to give this matter any further consideration. In effect the government said that the fate of the small retailer is no concern to them.
Finally I would draw the attention of the house to the fair trade laws of the United States. For a moment I should like to deal with the history of price maintenance and the growth of these fair trade laws in that country. Resale price maintenance was made illegal in the United States in the year 1900. I think it is very important to remember that date, because it was more than fifty years ago that that country did exactly what we are proposing to do today.
During the next thirty years, both consumers and retailers in the United States found that the conditions which this situation created were unsatisfactory. In 1931 the abolition of price maintenance was replaced by the first fair trade law, in the state of California. This law proved to be so satisfactory to both consumers and retailers that today forty-five out of the forty-eight states in the United States have replaced the abolition of price maintenance with fair trade laws.
i think it is obvious that the fair trade laws in the United States are just as satisfactory to consumers as they are to retailers, because there are more consumers than there are retailers, and consumers elect governments. If the fair trade laws had not proved to be more satisfactory to the consumers than the abolition of price maintenance, these forty-five governments would have been thrown out and the fair trade laws would have been thrown out with them.
The fact that the number of state governments that have introduced fair trade laws has increased from one to forty-five in the last twenty years demonstrates clearly, I believe, that the overwhelming majority of people in the United States are satisfied with the deal they get under the fair trade laws. It also demonstrates, I believe, that both the consumers and the retailers feel that they get a better deal under these laws than they got during that period when resale price maintenance was abolished.
I do not claim for a moment that laws which are satisfactory to the people of the United States are necessarily the best for Canada. However, I think we must remember that our economy and our buying habits are similar to those of the people of the United States. Therefore if we have any sense at all, and if we feel any responsibility to the people who elected us to this parliament, we should examine very carefully indeed their experience during .the past half century before embarking on new legislation of our own. We are planning to take a step which they
Combines Investigation Act took more than fifty years ago, a step which has proved unsatisfactory to 150 million people just to the south of us, during that fifty-year trial period. Today the step which they took more than fifty years ago has been almost unanimously revoked by the people of the United States. If we are to follow the course which this Liberal government now plans to take, we are going to turn back the clock by fifty years.
I believe the committee on resale price maintenance should be reconvened, for three reasons: First, so the small retailer can be given full opportunity to state his case in an-unbiased atmosphere; second, so a concerted attempt can be made to define the loss leader-and work out practical and enforceable legislation to curtail its abuses; third, so a thorough study of the fair trade laws of the United States can be made to determine if those laws can be adapted to the Canadian economy. I, for one, feel very confident that they can, because, as I have said, our economy is practically identical with the economy of the United States.
Having sat on this committee for nearly a month, I believe this legislation is hasty and ill-considered, and is merely an attempt to draw a red herring across the trail of the ever-increasing cost of living, in an effort to take the people's minds off .that very real problem. I believe that without a thorough and honest investigation of this whole problem, we are going to get legislation which 150 million people in the United States have tried and discarded after a trial lasting fifty years. Can we afford to ignore the lesson which has been learned by the most industrialized nation in the world today? I believe that the answer is an emphatic "no".

Mr. Speaker, I want to record an amazing incident which happened yesterday and which has been repeated in spots today. That is the trip taken to the land of make-believe under the guidance or direction of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson), aided and abetted in part or in whole by some on either side of this house. Let me assure you that it is a somewhat startling experience to be jolted from the corner of St. Denis and St. Catherine streets in Montreal, where I was mentally lost in the contemplation of an appealing store window, and find oneself propelled .to the Barbary coast. Yet that happened to me yesterday.
But not without avail, because, there, I was allowed to witness, in the fullest possible

Combines Investigation Act' bloom, the triumph of the merchandising and bargaining rights of the genus homo, tradesman, producer or retailer.
There, hidden behind a wide expanse of broad black backs manning the oars valiantly, if somewhat reluctantly, I was given to see with my own eyes the processes of free competitive trade, operating without interference from either state or producer. I was allowed to witness the broad play of competition at its fullest height, resulting in the privilege for the consumer to shop and bargain at his fancy, provided that he or she could preferably afford a four-in-hand, and did not mind adventures into trading which entailed flitting through the mire of the local common from butcher to draper, from draper to candlestick maker, to the spice man, the supplier of man's habiliments, to the carriage maker and the apothecary.
There 'mid the groans of unwilling labour recruited at some expense of human life, but with little other cost or remuneration, 1 relived during some minutes the enthralling appeal of free trade, unhampered, untrammelled and unfettered by what a sadly repentant world has come to denounce-if nowhere else at least in Canada-as the damning and soulsearing practice of resale price maintenance.
Having in a previous incarnation shown some disinclination to agree that the letters "R.P.M." must be interpreted as the mene, mene, tekel, upharsin of the consumer, my trip in the land of ministerial make-believe did me infinite good. It made me realize that even the best intentioned of us at times become forgetful of the bounties of Providence; and that, since under the leadership of this government and this party, our country has achieved an unparallelled position in the world and fob each of its citizens, it perhaps might be well to not disturb this order of things.
It has often been quoted in my own language that "Le mieux est l'ennemi du bien".
Upon my return from the gold coast and the Barbary coast, from my wanderings on the common of Boston, among the chandlers and tradespeople of New Amsterdam, and in the shadow of forts Lewis, Henry and George, it was with some degree of pleasure and with no inconsiderable feeling of pride in human achievement that my disillusioned eye roved over some of the gilded, becarpeted and luxuriously fronted emporia-even those without the further inducement of live models -which the minister of make-believe took some pains to delineate before this house yesterday.
Those of our colleagues, tradespeople, merchants, druggists, whom we had at first

accepted as sound people and men well regarded in their communities since they seemed to command the respect of the majority, which as the minister himself pointed out yesterday still rules-these colleagues, sir, upon my return regained some of their temporarily lost stature.
Clad as they had been in the land of make-believe in what to the fastidious were the somewhat repulsive and repellent tatters of Simon Legree and his French counterpart, Harpagon; twirling under the consumers' noses the implement for which the English equivalent fails me but which in French is known as "le tonneau des Danaides", behind which lurked the Medusa of resale price maintenance-they hardly qualified as representatives of the consuming public.
May I tell you, sir, that it was most gratifying upon my return to solid ground to be able to conclude that they are more than fully entitled to the original respect and tribute which has been paid each of them in his community.

Having returned from the land of make-believe may I dive headlong into the mother-sea of fact, there not to be submerged, I trust, as the McGregor fears, but to toe buoyed, I hope, upon the wave of concrete fact.
We are asked to legislate on resale price maintenance and to incorporate in our statutes an amendment to the Combines Investigation Act which will make it a criminal offence (a) to maintain or induce to maintain resale prices and (b) to refuse to supply goods as a consequence of refusal to maintain prices, each, I point out, being an offence in itself and quite independently to each other.
This measure has come as a considerable surprise in many quarters in view of recent Canadian history in the field of price investigations and in terms of the speech from the throne. In recent years we have had three definite and separate experiences of sorties into the field of prices. In 1948 the special committee on prices, consisting of members of this house, sat for almost four months. Its conclusions, after having delved deeply and at length into the question of prices and the causes for the then rise of prices, were that resale price maintenance, which might have been a small contributory factor, was certainly not such a factor as to warrant attention at any length.
If the prices committee did not at that time probe deeply into the question in spite of the length of the inquiry and in spite of

the ample time at its disposal, may I submit to you, sir, that this was done principally on the McGregor's advice on this matter.
I refer the house to page 210 of minutes of proceedings and evidence, No. 5, of the special committee on prices, Tuesday, February 17, 1948 in which, in answer to a question by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis)-, the witness, the McGregor, stated:
. . .we had no complaints in recent months and we had made no investigations in recent months. One reason may very well be, and it is a fact, that competition is working in most of the fields which are indicated in the four or five pages to which we referred yesterday.
The hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) interjected the following:
Items in the cost of living index.
The witness answered, "yes".
At page 213 during the same examination the witness was asked if there were any monopolies in the distributive trades or the manufacturing trades over the last ten years, and the answer, as found at page 213, was, "I do not think there have been in the distributive trades." At page 221-and I shall -come to this later because it has a very significant bearing-there is a question by the hon. member for Calgary East (Mr. Harkness) with respect to resale price maintenance. He said:
I would take it that you do not as a general rule look upon resale price maintenance as an inimical practice?
Further, and still as a question, he said:
I take it that from the fact that the situation exists you do not look on resale price maintenance as a bad practice as far as a large number of commodities are concerned. Is that correct?
The answer was:
I have taken a pretty strong attitude in this brief on the question of resale price maintenance. I realize that a case can be argued on the other side. If these issues were all capable of being referred to as black and white it would be a very much easier job of administration. Here is a case where I think you have to examine the particular commodity and the particular circumstances in every instance.
Later he said:
I would rather examine each case on its merits and then come to a conclusion.
I said there was some surprise at the terms of this legislation. May I refer hon. members to the speech from the throne in which the government suggested that it was about to introduce legislation "arising" out of the MacQuarrie report. I now submit that the bill before the house does not arise from the MacQuarrie report. It is a strict interpretation of and a rigid adherence to every single term and every single word of the conclusions of the MacQuarrie report.
Combines Investigation Act
Discussing the principle of the bill yesterday, the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) prefaced his remarks with the statement that he and his party took no strong attitude either for or against this measure. That, sir, was a statement which caused no great surprise on this side of the house or anywhere in the country. It is a statement which is very well in keeping with what is sometimes referred to with some levity as the Conservative philosophy.
Contrary to the hon. gentlemen I take a very strong view of this matter. I am in accord with the principle of legislation generally covered by the bill, but I am not fully in accord with its terms because the conclusions of the MacQuarrie report, now expressed in the terms of this bill, stem from premises which, in my humble opinion, have never been established.
The hon. gentlemen who were members of the special committee on combines realize that we have no evidence on the MacQuarrie investigation; but we do have evidence on one subject, namely the request made to industry when it was invited to appear before the MacQuarrie committee. I refer to page 663 et sequentia of Hansard of this year. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson), moving the motion to establish a joint committee to consider the interim report, quoted the letter which had been sent from Ottawa on July 7, 1950, to industry, and I quote part of this letter as follows:
To avoid any possible misunderstanding1, I desire to emphasize that no suggestions of amendments are being made to the committee for its consideration.
And further:
For its assistance in this study the committee is anxious to receive as soon as possible from organizations, firms and individuals whatever views they may wish to express upon matters within its terms of reference.
And still further:
In view of this the committee invites comments on this particular problem ... In particular, the committee would appreciate receiving extended comments on the tentative conclusion of the royal commission.
On the same page of Hansard a repetition to this effect:
The committee expresses a desire to secure as wide an expression of views as possible.
Later on, the minister went on to say at page 664:
The views that were submitted to the MacQuarrie committee were general views upon the subject of resale price maintenance.
And further: "This presentation of views", and so forth.
Now, sir, we do know that the committee had none of the evidence submitted to the MacQuarrie group before its eyes. But we

Combines Investigation Act also know this, and I bring it up in respect of the contention of the Minister of Justice, expressed many times during the committee's recent sittings but more particularly at pages 246, 252, 253 and 254 of our minutes, that the burden of proof to disprove the conclusions of the MacQuarrie committee rested on the shoulders of those who were appearing before the special house committee. I contend, sir, that a great deal rests on the interpretation of the word "views".
Following a price investigation by a special committee of this house in 1948, the conclusions of which did not in any way reach into resale price maintenance; following a royal commission subsequent to the report of this committee and extending into 1949, again with no definite conclusions as to objections to resale price maintenance; in 1950, without any action from a royal commission or a house committee; without any action for over twenty-five years by the commissioner of combines against resale price maintenance- and in spite of the fact that both the present and the former commissioners agree and admit that the present act would allow and justify prosecutions against resale price maintenance, on that very score and on that score alone-industry which had first been asked to submit to a third group, which has no judicial nor legislative capacity, its "views" on the matters, was now asked to destroy the conclusions of the MacQuarrie report.
I submit, sir, that industry, the merchant, the tradesman and the manufacturer, the butcher and the candlestick maker, must have submitted views; and my contention is supported no less by the fact that when the same people were again given the same invitation to submit their views before a committee of this house no less than a month and a half ago they again did so; but the Minister of Justice found it possible, found it necessary perhaps, in respect to his conscience or to his belief-and never would I contend that his conscience or his belief are not above reproach -and imperative, to state before the committee at every possible stage that the onus of proof to destroy the conclusions of the MacQuarrie committee was upon each and every one of the witnesses who appeared before us.
Now, sir, I have felt, and others in this house have felt, that perhaps their expressions of views should have been looked at and interpreted in the light of their general definition of life, not in the light of lawyers and legislators. Nothing perhaps substantiates this belief more than what one of the two largest labour groups in the country said at page 46 of our minutes on being asked whether they had appeared before the Mac-

Quarrie committee, and what argumentation they had submitted to that committee. They, through the voice of their public relations adviser, Dr. Forsey, stated as a preamble to their appearance before the committee, in Dr. Forsey's words:
Second, X want to make it very clear that the congress does not regard this legislation as of vast importance or likely to be of enormous effect upon the cost of living.
At one stage, sir, I waxed slightly curious and asked this question:
In so far as your report to the MacQuarrie committee is concerned, short though it may have been, was it substantially different from the brief we have before us?
The answer was:
It was very much shorter, and I think-in fact it simply contented itself with saying what our attitude was.
As I recall we did not present any argument.
Then I laboured the point slightly, and at times I was very meticulous. My question was:
Did your report to the MacQuarrie committee include any more substantial or concrete information than the brief which is before us this morning?
And the answer was:
Most decidedly not.
Yet, Mr. Speaker, I find at page 8 of the printed copy of the MacQuarrie report, under the heading "Submissions received" that, in general, retail associations, manufacturers, wholesalers and retailers were favourable to resale price maintenance, while on the contrary co-operatives, labour unions, farmers and consumer associations expressed opposition to the practice. Now, sir, I have dealt with one labour union. May I go on to a second witness from the same group of labour, the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada, who appeared before us. In the early part of their statement they said, on page 371 of the proceedings of the committee:
We would like to improve the standard of living: we are not interested in just going around seeking higher wages, and we are not sure whether amending the Combines Investigation Act would help that.
Further on they state:
We think if you set up a law of that sort in a positive sense, with a consumers' price board where these arrangements can be considered and approved in whatever form they may necessarily take, that we would be moving in a direction which would uphold the principle of free economy.
Then the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) tasked this question, as it appears on page 372 of the committee proceedings:
Q. Have you examined the draft bill on page 34 of the proceedings of this committee?
A. I have read the original draft.
Q. You will recall it purports to propose blanket prohibition on resale prices. Would you think that is a proper and desirable way of going about this matter that we have blanket prohibition, or if we

are going to have legislation on it should it be left to determine whether in the particular case the particular type of agreement is in the given circumstances harmful to the public interest or not?
