So the members of the committee and the members of this house are in this position today, that without having access to the evidence put before the MacQuarrie committee, this evidence being privileged, and having only the evidence submitted to the committee of this house on which to rely, we are asked to agree with conclusions reported by the MacQuarrie group, conclusions for which there is not the least vestige of a premise.
There were two groups who appeared before us, the protagonists and the antagonists. The protagonists claimed that resale price maintenance should be illegal because it deprives the consumer of his shopping rights, and it deprives the retailer of his full right to compete in prices. It is claimed that the alienation of this right is detrimental to the general interest-although no proof was submitted and proof to the contrary was admitted-in that the practice has led to higher prices.
The antagonists of this measure agree that resale price maintenance limits the consumer's bargaining power but not his right of discrimination between similar commodities. Rigidity of price has been claimed as one of the other factors in resale price maintenance. Price maintenance may be on only one, a few or many articles in a wide range. Variety, it has been contended and not disproved by the evidence in the record, assures price competition at all levels. A further contention was that prices are generally lower in the range of resale price-maintained goods, this being achieved through the phenomena of higher volume, more turnover, cheaper production cost, lesser margin and a lesser price.
Of course, sir, I was forgetting to bring into this discussion the evidence of one who has been termed by the hon. member for Coast-Capilano, and by others, as the "star witness" of the committee's investigation. This "star witness" made a series of pious statements, but he scrupulously avoided any reference to actual fact. From his slightly pursed lips cascaded an avalanche of "I believe", "I opine", "I think", "I hope", but never "I prove." I turn to page 388 of the record where the "star witness" said:
My very first major inquiry related to resale price maintenance. It was started in September, 1925...
Then he went on to describe his experience. This, sir, is in opposition to a very
Combines Investigation Act pertinent fact, because as you will see later the "star witness" for the protagonists held himself fully capable of discussing and determining the juridical portent of the bill now before us.
The "star witness", who had experience going as far back as 1925, declared in 1948- and I shall bring has evidence before this house in a moment-that after thinking over the point and discussing it with his associates during twenty-three years' experience, he was still unable to define or redefine the section of this act which would, in fairness to everyone, be the proper legislation against resale price maintenance.
At page 389 of the committee's proceedings our star witness stated:
If only a few of the manufacturers in any one field adopted the practice, and there were plenty others who did not, the damage to the consumer through such a limiting of price competition would not be devastating.
But, Mr. Speaker, nowhere in the 388 pages of evidence which precede this statement has it been proven that his contention was either true or untrue.
At page 390 the McGregor gives an "opinion", but this time he states it very clearly:
In my opinion, for the reasons I have indicated...
I should be deeply grateful, Mr. Speaker, to anyone in this house who would quote from this record what reasons have been indicated. The McGregor says:
In my opinion, for the reasons I have indicated, the combines act in its present form is not sufficient to prevent such action. The act needs amendment.
Further down on the same page he said:
The extension of the practice in recent years has been alarming. If it continues it will not be long before price control by manufacturers will become the rule in the distributive trade and price competition the exception . . .
But, gentlemen, you have all heard the pious reference, made in 1948, to the fact that over a period of years of the McGregor's experience, there was no lack of competition in the distributive trades. Now, of course, the extension of this practice "has been alarming". Indeed, so alarming has it become that later in his testimony the McGregor states that so far as he can ascertain-and again in his opinion I submit-over a period of almost thirty years, this practice, which at this stage has reached such "alarming" proportions, may have increased from 5 per cent of the volume of trade in 1925 to the alarming figure of perhaps 15 per cent in 1951. I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, that if we continue at this "alarming" rate almost three centuries would elapse before we were engulfed and thoroughly upset by this alarming phenomenon of resale price maintenance.

Combines Investigation Act
It is unfortunate, sir, that time prevents me from going through each of the opinions of our star witness, but here is one I should like to bring to your attention. It is another of the pious statements he made so frequently and with so little difficulty. Referring to the attitude of the "other fellow"-as he stated it-one wonders how many "peculiar" industries there are.
That word is in quotation marks even on the record, so there must have been a quotation either in his voice or in his script, although, Mr. Speaker, most members of this house iand all members of the committee know that it is easier for me to refer to the record than to his printed brief, because his printed brief was submitted only after he had put his contentions verbally on the record.
But please give your attention for a moment to the connotation of: One wonders how many "peculiar" industries there are in Canada; because turning back to page 597 of the record -again the McGregor being on the witness stand-he was asked in reference to one statement made by a witness in the retail drug trade, who had stated that it would be very difficult and in his own words, very rough, he being a manufacturer, if the business he had taken thirty years to build up could be left to be destroyed overnight by the decision of an independent dealer; the McGregor is being asked:
There is a case where a manufacturer says it is against his interest if retail price maintenance was not followed and he feels obviously very deeply about it. What would you say as to his argument?
Then the great, the ecstatic, the pious McGregor says:
I think this particular group is one again you would classify as one of the "peculiar" industries.

There is just this I want to say in conclusion. Many people have wondered why I am taking the attitude I am taking against this legislation. Let me say this to them. I represent in this house probably a greater number of shopkeepers and tradespeople than any other hon. member. Anyone who is familiar with St. Catherine, St. Lawrence, St. Denis, Amherst, Rachel, Mount Royal, Craig, St. James, Notre Dame and St. Paul streets in my riding will appreciate what I mean. The number and the interests of these people make it easy to understand why at times I have been perhaps too strong in upholding what I believe to be their viewpoint.
In one respect their situation is like mine. They, and I with them, may be convinced that the present bill is not a piece of legislation which will stand out among the achievements of this government. Yet they, and I with them, would hesitate to condemn the government because among its vast number of brilliant brain children it had allowed one to creep in which did not exactly scintillate.
Frankly, when I compare this bill with any of the other legislation that has been brought into the house by the government since I have been here, the bill does not gain stature. Frankly I dislike the bill. I dislike it as it is presented, although the addition of a few words would make it highly palatable. I dislike it because I fear the far-reaching effects which are not necessarily noticeable to the naked eye. In this respect I find myself in league with the small merchants of the country whose fears, well-founded or not, were clearly expressed during the sittings of the committee. Yet the addition of a few words would make it palatable. I find myself now in the position of having to determine my conduct henceforth.

Mr. Speaker, I feel I should say something with respect to this bill, because I was a member of the committee. It is true I became a member of it a week or ten days after it had begun its sittings. However, I was anxious to learn something about this matter because I entered the committee, as I stated in the committee itself, with an unbiased mind and without any idea of being an obstructionist so far as the legislation was concerned.
For the first few times I attended I listened with keen interest, because I wanted to find out something about the bill. It is not usual for a person to want to serve on a committee; but I went there for the purpose of learning. It is amazing to me to realize the number of people who do not know the definitions of the terms "resale price maintenance" or ."loss leader". We have heard criticism of the committee this afternoon, and I should like to add my criticism of it.
This legislation was announced in the speech from the throne. There were three evenings during the session when, for want of work to do, we adjourned at five o'clock. If this legislation had been brought in earlier in the session and a reasonable chance given to study it, then I would feel that I would know enough about it either to reject or support the bill. But at the present time I must say frankly that from the information I have received I cannot support it.
During the time we were on the committee several things happened that changed an unbiased mind into a mind that was beginning to form an opinion about this matter. The first thing that struck me was the fact that one morning some thousands of retailers, through their counsel, wanted to be heard before the committee. The ruling was: "No, we will not hear you. We have heard some other parts of your brief from some parent organization." Then I felt that when we were inquiring into something as important as this, and when thousands of retailers could

be turned away without a hearing the procedure of the committee was not democratic, and there was something wrong with it.
The next thing that bothered me a great deal was the attitude of the counsel to the committee. I have the greatest respect for the learned profession. I know they are criticized, as the members of my own profession are criticized. But while doctors develop a bedside manner, possibly lawyers develop a courtroom manner. I felt from the questioning of the counsel there one day that the witness was put in the position of a prisoner in the box who had committed a crime. In this instance the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Hees) and the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) protested vigorously about the attitude of the counsel to the committee. Next day it was much better. But I could not help feeling that a witness who came in to give his best opinion, whether for or against the legislation, should not be treated in that way.
Some of these things helped me to make up my mind, so far as the legislation is concerned. In fact the attitude of the committee brought one thing to my mind, and it was this: that as applied to the retailers it might have been suitable if they had been told, "Abandon hope, all ye retailers who enter here". That is what was absolutely wrong about this committee, in addition to the fact that it was brought into being too late.
There were certain things about which I wanted to get information. I wanted to find out certain things about matters in which those people were concerned. One of the things mentioned in their brief indicated that there was in their minds some question of price fixing or combines in connection with obtaining cement, and that the western people were concerned about the trouble in getting fertilizers and the position in which the agencies were placed. I could obtain no information on those things.
The problem facing every person in this country today is the high cost of living. It has been said half a dozen times this afternoon that this legislation was brought in to try to make the people believe this government was doing something about the cost of living. They have been bitterly criticized on that account, and the reaction of the people in five by-elections shows that they are very much interested in the high cost of living.
I feel that the committee did not have the time or opportunity to make a proper study of this legislation. The matter is too big and too important. If it is going to affect the small retailer as we believe it will, we should

give further study to it and try to bring in a bill that will be the best possible for this country.
The hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Hees) referred this afternoon to the fair trade laws in the United States. Forty-five states have enacted these laws. In the United States the consumer, the retailer and the manufacturer all seem to be quite happy and satisfied. Something like that is worth studying before we hurriedly bring in a bill of this type in what I hope are the closing days of the session. It should receive more study instead of a heated debate for twenty-four hours in this chamber and then pushed through to a vote. As has been suggested this afternoon, we will be studying this matter later when we see its consequences upon the public.
I stated that very few people are really aware what resale price maintenance means. As authority for this I will take the report of the MacQuarrie committee. I find it stated in the interim report that resale price maintenance means the right of the manufacturer of a product to establish the price at which it will be sold. I think that should be placed in simple language before the people of this country. It is not an agreement between a manufacturer and his competitors to keep up prices. We should be clear on that matter. I was interested to note that in the committee certain things continually came into the discussion, rather than the broad picture of all commodities in which we would be interested. It was amazing to find that the one thing that was recurring was aspirin and the other was mixmasters. Then there was one other, the cost of dry cell batteries, and also paint brushes. I shall have something to say about aspirin and its effect on the pharmaceutical trade later on.
I come now to this matter of loss leaders. The minister sat opposite to me most of the time in the committee when we were talking about this matter of loss leaders. It is generally agreed that it is a vicious practice in merchandising. I went to the MacQuarrie committee report to obtain a definition of loss leader, and the following will be found on page 25:
The second practice, called the "loss-leader" device, is an aggressive weapon designed to attract customers for a whole range of goods by a particular part of selective and excessive price-cutting. Usually a well-known brand is used as "loss-leader" and it is sold at a price which has no direct relation to cost and may even result in a net loss.
I remember that this matter of loss leader was under discussion in the committee one day and I made the remark that it was difficult to legislate against something that was hard to define. I am not going to repeat what
Combines Investigation Act has been said since this debate started, but I should like to refer again to the MacQuarrie report which admits that price maintenance prevents two possible forms of monopolistic practice which tend to produce unreasonable retail prices; first, the use of monopoly power at the retail level and, second, the loss leader device.
We all admit, and we found out in the committee, that the loss-leader type of merchandising is a vicious practice. The minister himself admitted that in the committee; I remember that he took my word that it is difficult to legislate against something which cannot be defined. I came upon a most amazing thing on the last page of the MacQuarrie report. This type of merchandising is a vicious practice, and I quote from the MacQuarrie report as follows:
As to the "loss-leader" device, the committee believes that it is a monopolistic practice which does not promote general welfare and therefore considers that it is not compatible with the public interest.
That is true so far as it goes.
However, we do not believe that it presents any immediate danger: extreme forms of price-cutting are not very likely in this period of inflation and relative scarcity. Moreover, we are convinced that there can be found other effective and more desirable methods of controlling the "loss-leader" than minimum resale price maintenance.
This last statement is important.
Present circumstances afford time to make a careful study of such methods and the committee, therefore, does not think it imperative to make an immediate and hasty recommendation regarding that practice.
If the loss-leader device in merchandising is a vicious practice, why is something not being done about it now? If the answer is in the present legislation on combines, why has something not been done before this?
There are advantages in resale price maintenance. One has to admit that. In practising resale price maintenance the manufacturer places the small merchant in a better competitive position because the practice of resale price maintenance is against the loss-leader practice. The other people whom we must consider are the consumers. There is something to be said for resale price maintenance so far as the consumer is concerned. This creates a common price for the same article no matter where it is bought.
Another way in which resale price maintenance is valuable is that the consumer is ensured against high prices in times of scarcity. These things should be considered. We should not become prejudiced against something that will really do good in the end.
There is another matter. We have spoken a great many times about competition. I

Combines Investigation Act have always been interested in name brands.
I have found it impossible to be an authority on every single commodity that I buy. I could not judge a watch, and I certainly am a poor judge of textiles. So many things enter into our life that we have come to look upon the name brand as a mark of quality.
I certainly could not look into a watch and tell that that was the best movement I could find in keeping with my purse. Therefore I depend on certain established brand names, since I look on them as a mark of quality. I have found during my life that it is better to buy something that has a brand on it because you are sure of the type of commodity that you are buying, rather than to go adventuring in certain unnamed types of merchandise. I have found it a protection in so far as I am concerned because I could not afford to buy something that was useless and would not last. I have taken a watch as a comparison, but in the whole field of watches you can start with well known brands like Waltham and Elgin and go all the way down the list until you find a name brand that will fit your purse. Behind it there is a guarantee of quality by a reputable company.
There were some other things that bothered me so far as the deliberations of the committee were concerned. I wondered with respect to the legislation now being introduced whether it would be possible to enforce something like that. Could it possibly be done by law? I came to the conclusion that it would require more men than we have in the armed forces at the present time to enforce a law of this type. I am also very much concerned about the cost of living, and I came to the conclusion that this measure will have little or no effect in so far as the cost of living is concerned. When I had the opportunity I went into many stores, and I was certainly seeking for the truth. I found that very many things sold in the stores have nothing to do with resale price maintenance.
The first person I went to was a grocer, and altogether I visited several stores. By the word "grocer" I mean people who sell food, because I include them all; and the odd butcher shop carries a line of groceries. I could only find three or four items in the whole stock carried by stores engaged in selling groceries that were price-maintained, and they were mainly luxury items. I found that cocoa and some food products such as salad dressing and cream cheese are price-maintained, and that so far as all the rest are concerned very few products are price-maintained. Food is a very important commodity at the present time. Everybody is interested in the cost of food.

Then I made further inquiries as to such commodities as sugar, flour, suits of clothes, ladies dresses and wearing apparel; and very few were price-maintained with the possible exception of men's wear. A well known brand of hat or a certain type of shoe was price-maintained. However, there is nothing which compels the buyer to resort to articles which are price-maintained. He can purchase if he so desires certain articles that are not price-maintained in every kind of commodity.
I next visited people engaged in the tobacco trade, and there one finds a certain type of individual in small stores all throughout the country. I was amazed at the number of veterans, some of whom were pensionable, who had started little stores in an effort to re-establish themselves. You would find them running a service station and selling a little tobacco. I found widows and persons who are physically unfit running little stores in outlying parts of the town. They did not carry very much stock but one of the things they carried was tobacco. Then I ascertained the number of retail tobacco people in Canada, and I found there are 90,000 outlets. This matter was not put before the joint committee and I lacked information and still do so far as the tobacco trade is concerned.
Personally I am concerned about these little people who are running stores. Then I investigated the percentage of profit made by those with little stores and I found that those retailing tobacco make a gross profit of 10-48 per cent, which in these days is not exorbitant. The public are inclined to blame the tobacconists for high prices when they are not at all to blame, and the amazing thing is the fact that 60 per cent of the price of cigarettes goes to the government.
With reference to mixmasters, I remember the day in the house when we were discussing the budget and we appealed to the government not to put a further tax on essential household articles such as electric appliances. Additional government taxation and increased sales tax brings up the price of such commodities, and the public surely should not be led to believe that the increase in the prices of these commodities is due to the fact that their resale price is maintained. The government is making a lot of money out of it. The government takes most of the money in so far as their price is concerned.
I was amazed, and in this I make no appeal for sympathy, at the number of veterans who are conducting small stores trying to eke out a living. I am interested in the person with the small store. He should have a chance to live. When I found veterans running stores trying to eke out

a living because of the size of their pensions or war veterans allowance, then I certainly felt that nothing should be done to prejudice their position. I then went to see people in the jewelry trade. I learned in the committee that practically no watches are manufactured in Canada. There is only one type of watch manufactured in this country, the Westclox, which with all due respect to the firm is a cheaper type of watch. All other watches that we have in Canada are made in Switzerland, although some of them are cased in this country.
That is one thing we found out in the committee but, as I said before, there is a measure of protection in the names of certain types of the better grades of watches. I went to a jeweler and said: "What do you think about this thing? How does it affect you?" He did not speak for a minute. He just looked at me, went to the window and took out two diamonds in cases. They were obviously engagement rings. He said: "You must remember that the small jeweler has not behind him a name like Ryrie-Birks; we have to depend on certain branded types of merchandise in order to be sure." When the average young man goes to purchase such a thing he is certainly in a jittery state and is no judge of diamonds. This jeweler showed me one name brand of diamond he sold and said, "I can guarantee this, and the customer will know what he is getting when he buys this brand." Then he showed me the other diamond that had no name and I said, "I do not know whether or not it is good". He said, "I just wanted to assure you that it is not. It is not worth half as much as the other but I can sell it for twice as much, and no young man will be aware of what is happening." Therefore so far as the jewelry trade is concerned, and I include in that silverware and certain other commodities, we come back to the point that the average buyer is no judge. One could not possibly be a judge of all commodities, and when we go to buy jewelry or anything in a jewelry store we have to depend on certain name products.
The next people concerned were the druggists. Of all retailers the druggists have certainly taken it on the jaw so far as criticism is concerned. Everybody seems to be after the druggists. I noticed that people generally seem to have adopted the attitude of the committee because when I asked certain people about the druggists-and again I honestly say I have made inquiries as to the public attitude-they always said to me, "What about aspirin?" Surely something more is sold in a drug store than aspirin. Let us go into this aspirin question, because
Combines Investigation Act I am sick and tired of people saying to me: "What about aspirin?" I am going to tell the story. Let us scotch this thing once and for all. About 40 years ago, or sometime later, when salicylic acid was discovered, one company put it out first under the trade name "aspirin", and the name was registered. But all other pharmaceutical houses sooner or later followed suit, and the peculiar thing was that they named their product "aspirin". I do not know why. They thought that the chemist who discovered it called it "aspirin" and they followed suit, and all the pharmaceutical houses throughout America, in fact, placed this product on the market under the name "aspirin". For thirty or forty years nothing was done about it; aspirin was the name. It became the name of the household commodity. The name was common, and owing to the advertising on the radio by one well-known company the name became very, very well known.
A short time ago the Bayer people clamped down and said: "This is our trade name. You cannot sell that product. If any drug store sells this product, or if any of you people or other pharmaceutical houses put it out with the name 'aspirin' on the bottle, then you are subject to a fine under the laws affecting trade marks". So all the other pharmaceutical houses had to hustle around and find new names. So they picked on the names like A.S.A., acetylsalicylic acid, cetasai, cetyloid, and all that sort of thing. But after 40 years it is pretty hard for the public to start learning these names. Therefore when you go into the drug store and ask for aspirin the druggist is legally compelled to give you Bayer's aspirin and nothing else. If any consumer knows that he can walk into a drug store and ask for acetylsalicylic acid, 5 grains or A.S.A. tablets, or cetasai, or cetyloid, or any of the names, then he can get it at about one-quarter of the price. There is no doubt about that. But that was, I was going to say, sharp practice so far as the firm was concerned. It certainly was pretty sharp business practice. I understand that the story is this. No other country in the world permits this law in regard to aspirin. The name has been accepted in Canada, and when you ask for aspirin you have to buy Bayer's. There is some reason behind that. I understand-I may be subject to correction-that when this matter came before the Supreme Court of Canada the pharmaceutical people thought there was nothing to it and they did not make an appearance and judgment was given in favour of the Bayer people.
I am very much concerned, Mr. Speaker, about the position of the druggists. As I said, they have been open to a great deal of criti-

The public are being taught to believe that they are people who insist on tremendously high margins of profit in connection with the manufacturing pharmaceutical people themselves. But I want you to remember this when you talk about the druggists. They occupy a dual position. They are professional people, and they are merchants. Nobody can run a drug store unless he has had four years' training. This is demanded by the laws of the province. As I said, they have a dual position. Owing to the fact that they are professional men I think that some of the criticism is entirely unjustified. It may be that there are certain commodities which do cost a great deal, but I want ypu to remember that so far as the druggists and drugstore items are concerned, the people seem to have an idea that they should buy these items at the old prices. They are not taking into consideration either high costs or rising prices, and they have never considered the question of inflation.
One might put it this way. There was a time when the public generally thought that a box of pills was worth 50 cents, no matter what it contained, and they are still looking for a 50-cent box of pills. Conditions in the drug trade have absolutely changed. As I said in the committee, there was a time when they were apothecaries, and the doctors were inclined to write prescriptions with probably ten and twelve ingredients in them. The druggists had to make all the ointments themselves. They had to roll the pills and do all that sort of stuff, but conditions are quite different now. A lot of these commodities used by doctors are put out in a bottle, possibly with the prescription on the side of the bottle, showing the potency in unit strength. When a doctor, being interested in his patient, wishes to prescribe he naturally wants to get the best product possible. I do not mind bringing Arms into this debate, because firms like Burroughs Wellcome, Parke-Davis, Eli Lilly and so forth, are people who cannot afford to put out a product which is lacking in potency or in unit strength; and doctors in prescribing sometimes specify products of a certain type of the company which will make a certain pill of a certain tincture, or a pharmaceutical.
That is very important. The public should understand that. I think it was shown in one of the briefs presented from England that there was an outgrowth of people who had sort of horned into this trade, particularly in the proprietary preparations, and in consideration of this one must remember and the public must be taught-and I find it in my own practice so often-that if you are going to get the best for a patient you must be careful what type of thing you prescribe.

Let us assume, as I have used the heart case before, that you have a heart case requiring tincture of digitalis. Certainly if a man appears in my office with swollen legs and is puffy on exertion, and that sort of thing, and I want to prescribe digitalis I want the best tincture that is available. It is not sufficient just to say tinctura digitalis, because these things are not measured in potency in this country. That is true. It does not seem to be a matter of protecting the doctor or the public in the matter of rating the potent strength of these commodities, the unit strength. Therefore you give them the best possible thing you can buy, and sometimes it costs more.
I listed in the committee for the purpose of explanation a preparation like vitamin B complex. You will pay what you might consider a high price for that preparation, possibly $5 for a hundred tablets made by a highly reputable firm, who place their integrity on the prescription that is on the front of the bottle. But you can buy these from certain wholesale people without any prescription on the bottle for probably a quarter of the price. These people are always very cagey; they never put the prescription or the unit strength on the bottle, but to the public it is all the one thing. They are getting the one drug. These are matters that are worthy of consideration.
I cannot see where any change in the small percentage of resale price-maintained consumer goods that are sold in drug stores is going to be a factor in the cost of living, because it has the advantage of putting a ceiling above as well as a floor beneath, particularly on commodities like drugs. It is not a factor in the cost of living when you come to a bill like this and find that the per capita expenditure in all drug stores on items that are price marked or otherwise over the year 1950 was $16.50 for each person in Canada on drugs, and that includes all the commodities in a drug store. But again I say that if you do consider some of these things as being high in price, nobody is compelled to buy resale price-maintained goods.
The main conclusion in the MacQuarrie report about resale price maintenance certainly is not true so far as I am concerned. I heard the minister talking about cough syrup, back plasters and cough lozenges, but he did not mention Lydia Pinkham. Remember that these things are not prescribed by any doctor who has a reputation he wishes to protect. A reputable doctor in good standing certainly is not going to prescribe Smith Brothers cough lozenges. I ask how you are going to control prices of the so-called proprietary medicines. Naturally I do not hold that proprietary medicines serve a

purpose; being a doctor I cannot feel that they do. But I do say that if the public want to buy them they have the right to do so. Let us take a commodity like Lydia Pinkham's vegetable compound which is marked at $2 and is price-maintained. Where are you going to arrive if you go back to find the value of the drugs in this commodity? These formulas are registered in Ottawa, and that would be easily ascertained. Again I say that I do not want to be put in the position of criticizing these goods, because when you criticize them it sometimes acts as a boost. After all, the public have the right to buy these things if they want to buy them.
1 come back again to that matter of quality brands. This afternoon several speakers mentioned this aspect of the problem. There is no occupation where quality brands are more important than that of a druggist. There are two objectives in resale price maintenance. So far as drugs are concerned, the first is the prestige of the manufacturer and the high grade article he puts out. The other objective is the protection of the druggist by assuring him a proper margin. It protects the consumer because the prices are the same in all stores. If it were not for resale price maintenance the small merchant would be at the mercy of the chain drug store.
I have aproached this matter as conscientiously as any person ever could. If this were something that would cut down the cost of living, I would be in favour of it. I have not been convinced that it is going to accomplish that object. I do not believe it is going to make any impact on the cost of living, and the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) admits that. It is going to destroy the small businesses which are so important in all the towns throughout the country. It is going to kill the small druggist who is furnishing a service in the outlying districts. The larger businesses will probably absorb some of the small merchants. The chain stores and departmental stores will have a big advantage. If resale price maintenance is wrong in so far as the drug trade is concerned, then it has been wrong for a long time. It has taken forty-one years for this to come to the surface. If it is going to be of such tremendous advantage to the public, as a member of the opposition I will say it has taken the government a long time to find out that this practice is harmful to the Canadian consumer. Do not forget that pharmacists are professional men. They should have more protection than will be afforded in the legislation we have before us. Back of that is the question of the health of the Canadian people. In the committee Mr. McGregor almost made a statement-I accused him of saying it and he said
Combines Investigation Act the words were put in his mouth-about wiping out the small, inefficient stores. We cannot afford to wipe out the small, inefficient stores.
The druggists have been forced into the position of selling other commodities. Some of them have been forced to sell sandwiches, lunches and in the outlying districts, even groceries. These stores still furnish a service to the community. I have never found a druggist who would not get up at two or three o'clock in the morning to fill a prescription. I dislike the fact that this legislation seems to be aimed at the druggists. I am tired, Mr. Speaker, of hearing people say, "Well, what about aspirin?"

C'est une contradiction a noter. Dans cette fausse position, les partisans du colonel Drew posent en champions de la liberte du commerce. Mais la liberte du commerce consiste, semble-t-il, a laisser aux mar-chands detaillants le soin de vendre leurs merchandises a leur convenance. L'opposition ne l'entend pas de cette fagon. Elle perd done le credit de ses campagnes oratoires en faveur de la fixation des prix par le gouvernement. En effet, si le gouvernement decide enfin de proteger le consommateur par intervention legislative, sa loi de eontrole s'appliquera a tous les producteurs de l'industrie ou de l'agriculture. Quelle belle occasion pour le gouvernement de confondre ses adversaires, en donnant satisfaction au peuple qui compte sur lui pour obtenir protection contre tous les profi-teurs. Pourquoi remettre d plus tard une action aussi necessaire au bien-etre des classes labo-rieuses!
Trois enquetes ont demontre que le public etait exploite honteusement par le privilege qu'avaient les grands manufacturiers de fixer le prix de vente au detail de leurs merchandises; et malgre cela, les conservateurs trouvent moyen de se faire les defenseurs de ces ex-ploiteurs de la grande masse des consomma-teurs canadiens.
